PDC-01: Control objectives, feedback and feedforward

Overview

Assumed: steady material and energy balances.

Control keeps a process near a desired operating condition while its inputs change. A heated, well-mixed tank shows the difference between rejecting a disturbance and following a new target, and between correcting an observed error and anticipating its cause.

Intuition

A steady design tells us how much heat is needed at one condition. It does not make that heat supply adjust when the feed becomes colder. Feedback watches the result; feedforward watches a disturbance and predicts the required correction.

The controlled variable is the quantity to regulate, the manipulated variable is an input we can adjust, and a disturbance is an input change outside this controller's authority. A set point is the desired controlled-variable value.

Follow a cold-feed disturbance through the tank. Colder liquid first reduces the energy arriving each second; stored energy then falls, so the tank cools. Feedback detects that temperature fall and raises heating. Feedforward measures the colder feed and raises heating before the tank needs to cool. This causal sequence explains why feedback needs a changed measurement and why feedforward needs a model of the disturbance's effect.

Derivation

Step 1: identify the physical balance. Let liquid density be ρ\rhoρ, specific heat capacity cpc_pcp​, tank volume VVV, equal inlet/outlet volumetric flow qqq, feed temperature T0T_0T0​, tank/outlet temperature TTT, and heating rate QQQ. Assume perfect mixing, constant properties and volume, no reaction, heat loss or appreciable mixer work. Energy accumulation gives

ρVcpdTdt=ρqcp(T0−T)+Q.(1)\rho Vc_p\frac{dT}{dt}=\rho qc_p(T_0-T)+Q.\tag{1}ρVcp​dtdT​=ρqcp​(T0​−T)+Q.(1)

Reason: inflowing liquid brings sensible heat, the outlet carries heat at the tank temperature, and the heater adds energy. At steady target temperature TspT_{sp}Tsp​, set the derivative to zero:

Qs=ρqcp(Tsp−T0s).(2)Q_s=\rho qc_p(T_{sp}-T_{0s}).\tag{2}Qs​=ρqcp​(Tsp​−T0s​).(2)

Here subscript sss denotes a steady operating value. This is the heat requirement, not a controller algorithm.

Step 2: define feedback. A sensor reports measured temperature TmT_mTm​; the controller forms error e=Tsp−Tme=T_{sp}-T_me=Tsp​−Tm​ and commands the final control element, which changes QQQ. If TmT_mTm​ is too low, more heating should raise TTT; if it is too high, heating should fall.

Reason: the measurement closes a path from process output back to process input. Sensor and actuator dynamics are part of that path.

Step 3: define feedforward. If T0T_0T0​ is measured, an ideal heat command for this simplified tank is

Qff=ρqcp(Tsp−T0).(3)Q_{ff}=\rho qc_p(T_{sp}-T_0).\tag{3}Qff​=ρqcp​(Tsp​−T0​).(3)

Reason: replacing the unknown disturbance by its measured value cancels its contribution to the energy balance. With this exact model and instantaneous heating, ρVcpT˙=ρqcp(Tsp−T)\rho Vc_p\dot T=\rho qc_p(T_{sp}-T)ρVcp​T˙=ρqcp​(Tsp​−T), so a tank initially at the fixed target stays there.

Motivation and explanation

Regulator control holds the target fixed while rejecting a disturbance. Servo control changes the output to follow a changed target. The same loop can perform both; they are different tests of its behaviour.

An on/off thermostat switches heating on below its switching range and off above it. Heat storage and switching can sustain a temperature cycle even with constant outside conditions; feedback alone does not guarantee a smooth response.

Feedback can respond to unmeasured disturbances but requires an error or measurement change before acting. Feedforward can act before an output error, but only for measured disturbances and only as well as the model and actuator permit. Combining them lets feedback correct residual modelling error.

Control objectives include safety constraints, operability and profitability. Inventory, pressure and temperature limits support operation; product quality and energy use support economics. Ordinary regulatory control is only one protective layer. Heater capacity, valve limits and process design constrain what any controller can achieve.

Worked example

Take water with ρ=1000\rho=1000ρ=1000 kg m−3^{-3}−3, cp=4200c_p=4200cp​=4200 J kg−1^{-1}−1 K−1^{-1}−1 and q=0.010q=0.010q=0.010 m3^33 s−1^{-1}−1. Holding Tsp=50T_{sp}=50Tsp​=50 °C with T0s=20T_{0s}=20T0s​=20 °C requires Qs=1.260Q_s=1.260Qs​=1.260 MW. If the inlet falls to 151515 °C, the model requires 1.4701.4701.470 MW, an increase of 0.2100.2100.210 MW.

A regulator makes that correction while keeping the target at 505050 °C. A servo instead reacts to an operator changing the target. A real feedforward command would also need accurate flow and properties, sufficient heat capacity and allowance for sensor/actuator delay.

The extra heating has a simple meaning: the heat-capacity flow rate is ρqcp=42000\rho qc_p=42000ρqcp​=42000 W K−1^{-1}−1, so every kelvin lost from the feed needs that much extra power. The tank's stored heat determines how quickly an uncompensated error develops; it does not change the final power required. The ideal feedforward law preserves an existing fixed target, but an instantaneous target change cannot make stored liquid jump to a new temperature.

Link to other topics

The same accumulation balance will give the tank time constant. Feedback design then depends on the combined dynamics of tank, sensor and final control element.

Conclusion

Choose the objective and available measurements before choosing a controller. A correct steady heat requirement is the starting point for a dynamic control model.

PDC-02: Choosing variables and interpreting distillation loops

Overview

Assumed: distillation equipment and the roles of reflux, reboiling and condensation.

Control-variable labels depend on the chosen process boundary and available actuators. A distillation column makes this concrete: pressure and inventories must be maintained while product compositions are regulated.

Intuition

A vessel level is an inventory signal: it tells us whether material is accumulating. A tray temperature can be a composition signal: at a known pressure and suitable mixture conditions, a changed composition changes the boiling temperature. These measurements solve different problems even though their loops interact.

To choose an actuator, imagine moving its valve and follow what happens to the measured quantity. Opening distillate withdrawal removes liquid from the drum directly. Increasing reflux also removes drum liquid, but sends it back into the column and changes separation. Reserving different actuators for inventory and quality avoids asking one valve to satisfy two independent objectives at once; it does not eliminate interactions.

Derivation

Step 1: specify boundaries. Include the column, condenser, reflux drum and reboiler in the process boundary. The feed is an external input; reflux is an internal circulation but remains an actuator-driven input to the column subsystem.

Step 2: connect inventory to a balance. If MDM_DMD​ is drum liquid mass and m˙C\dot m_Cm˙C​, m˙R\dot m_Rm˙R​, m˙D\dot m_Dm˙D​ are condensate, reflux and distillate mass flow rates, then

dMDdt=m˙C−m˙R−m˙D.(4)\frac{dM_D}{dt}=\dot m_C-\dot m_R-\dot m_D.\tag{4}dtdMD​​=m˙C​−m˙R​−m˙D​.(4)

Reason: drum level can remain steady only when inflow matches the two outflows. Adjusting distillate flow changes accumulation directly. An analogous base balance connects bottom level to bottoms withdrawal.

Step 3: read the five loops. PC, LC and TC mean pressure, level and temperature controller. Dotted lines carry measurement/control information; solid lines carry material.

Controlled measurement Manipulated input in this arrangement Physical reason
Column overhead pressure Condenser coolant flow Heat removal changes condensation and vapour inventory
Reflux-drum level Distillate withdrawal Removes accumulated condensate
Upper-column temperature Reflux flow Changes internal liquid flow and upper separation
Lower-column temperature Reboiler steam flow Changes boil-up and lower separation
Column-base level Bottoms withdrawal Removes accumulated bottom liquid

Reason: each information path terminates at a valve that can influence its measurement. This is one possible pairing, not a universal rule.

At the old steady state, the drum inflow and outflows balance. If condensate inflow rises while both withdrawals stay fixed, the positive imbalance integrates into increasing mass and level. With no level-dependent outflow in this simplified balance, a higher level alone does not remove that imbalance. The level controller supplies the restoring action by changing withdrawal. A temperature loop instead changes internal contacting and vapour–liquid equilibrium, so its physical pathway is different.

Motivation and explanation

The desired variables may be top and bottom composition, while the measured variables are tray temperatures. Temperature is an inferential measurement of composition; it must be justified for the mixture and pressure. Pressure changes, multicomponent feeds or weak temperature sensitivity can undermine the inference.

Feed flow, composition and temperature often act as disturbances because an upstream unit determines them. They become manipulated variables only if this controller is allowed to adjust them. Reflux changes both inventories and separation, and steam changes several tray conditions: five loops do not imply five independent processes.

Worked example

Suppose the reflux-drum level rises while its set point is unchanged. Increasing distillate withdrawal makes the right side of the drum balance smaller, opposing accumulation. Reducing reflux could also lower the level, but would disturb upper-column separation; the pairing above reserves reflux for the temperature loop.

If pressure rises, the pressure loop can increase condenser cooling within its available range. A temperature loop should not interpret every simultaneous temperature change as composition error: boiling temperature also depends on pressure.

Link to other topics

Phase equilibrium explains why pressure and composition affect tray temperature. Dynamic inventory balances explain why level loops are essential even when product specifications are the main economic objective.

Conclusion

A control structure is a set of physically justified measurement–actuator pairings. Its adequacy depends on interactions and dynamics as well as steady separation performance.

PDC-03: CSTR variable identification and dynamic model closure

Overview

Assumed: well-mixed reactor mass and energy balances.

For a jacketed CSTR carrying out A→BA\rightarrow BA→B, identify inputs, outputs and states before simplifying its balances. Measurements and manipulability are engineering choices, rather than intrinsic properties of a variable.

Intuition

The reactor stores material and energy. Feed and coolant conditions drive its behaviour; concentration, temperature and volume describe its evolving contents. A product-flow valve is physically on an outlet line but may be treated as a model input because its position changes reactor accumulation.

Derivation

Step 1: label the equipment. Let q0,q1q_0,q_1q0​,q1​ be feed/product volumetric flow rates, cA0,cA1c_{A0},c_{A1}cA0​,cA1​ their concentrations of A, T0,T1T_0,T_1T0​,T1​ their temperatures, VVV reactor volume, wcw_cwc​ coolant mass flow, and Tci,TcoT_{ci},T_{co}Tci​,Tco​ coolant inlet/outlet temperatures.

Step 2: state one plausible control assignment. Let the upstream process determine q0,cA0,T0q_0,c_{A0},T_0q0​,cA0​,T0​. Use product withdrawal to control volume and coolant flow to control reactor temperature.

Variable Model role under this assignment Typical measurement and use
q0q_0q0​ Disturbance input Flowmeter; monitor or use for compensation
cA0c_{A0}cA0​ Disturbance input Online analyser or sampled analysis; may be unmeasured online
T0T_0T0​ Disturbance input Temperature sensor
q1q_1q1​ Manipulated input Flowmeter and product valve/pump
cA1c_{A1}cA1​ Output/state Analyser or sampled analysis; possible quality target
T1T_1T1​ Controlled output/state Temperature sensor; coolant-flow loop
VVV Controlled output/state Level measurement with geometry conversion
wcw_cwc​ Manipulated input Coolant flowmeter and valve
TciT_{ci}Tci​ Disturbance input Temperature sensor; utility condition
TcoT_{co}Tco​ Output of coolant subsystem Temperature sensor; heat-duty monitoring

Reason: disturbances enter from outside the selected authority, whereas actuators can be commanded. An input can be measured; an output can be unmeasured. If q1q_1q1​ instead follows a gravity-outflow law, it becomes a dependent output and a different actuator must regulate volume.

Step 3: write the balances. For constant equal liquid densities, no volume change on mixing, and positive reaction-consumption rate r(cA1,T1)r(c_{A1},T_1)r(cA1​,T1​) per reactor volume,

V˙=q0−q1,d(VcA1)dt=q0cA0−q1cA1−Vr.(5)\dot V=q_0-q_1,\qquad \frac{d(Vc_{A1})}{dt}=q_0c_{A0}-q_1c_{A1}-Vr.\tag{5}V˙=q0​−q1​,dtd(VcA1​)​=q0​cA0​−q1​cA1​−Vr.(5)

Reason: use the extensive amount VcA1Vc_{A1}VcA1​ while volume can change. Expand its derivative and substitute the volume balance:

Vc˙A1=q0(cA0−cA1)−Vr.(6)V\dot c_{A1}=q_0(c_{A0}-c_{A1})-Vr.\tag{6}Vc˙A1​=q0​(cA0​−cA1​)−Vr.(6)

Reason: well-mixed withdrawal removes solute and solvent proportionally, so its direct concentration contribution cancels.

For constant liquid properties, negligible pressure work and mixer heating, heat of reaction ΔHr\Delta H_rΔHr​ per mole reacted, and positive cooling duty QcQ_cQc​,

ρVcpT˙1=ρq0cp(T0−T1)+(−ΔHr)Vr−Qc.(7)\rho Vc_p\dot T_1=\rho q_0c_p(T_0-T_1)+(-\Delta H_r)Vr-Q_c.\tag{7}ρVcp​T˙1​=ρq0​cp​(T0​−T1​)+(−ΔHr​)Vr−Qc​.(7)

Reason: the volume derivative cancels the outlet sensible-energy term in the same way. Exothermic reaction has ΔHr<0\Delta H_r<0ΔHr​<0 and therefore adds heat. Close the model with a rate law, geometry, valve/flow relations and a heat-transfer model. For example, Qc=UAh(T1−Tc)Q_c=UA_h(T_1-T_c)Qc​=UAh​(T1​−Tc​) uses heat-transfer coefficient UUU, area AhA_hAh​ and a representative jacket temperature TcT_cTc​; a dynamic jacket needs its own energy balance.

The outlet-flow cancellation is physical, not just convenient algebra. Removing a small portion of perfectly mixed liquid removes the same fraction of A as of total volume, leaving the remaining concentration unchanged at that instant. It still changes VVV, so subsequent feed dilution and reaction per stored amount can evolve differently. A concentration is a ratio; the amount balance and volume balance must agree before an equation for that ratio is trustworthy.

Model closure means being able to calculate every right-hand side from the current states and specified inputs. Knowing V,cA1,T1V,c_{A1},T_1V,cA1​,T1​ is insufficient if rrr or QcQ_cQc​ is still unknown. A rate law supplies rrr; a heat-transfer relation and, if needed, a jacket energy balance supply QcQ_cQc​. Each additional stored quantity needs its own initial condition and balance.

Motivation and explanation

Steady state sets all accumulation terms to zero. It does not remove the need for the rate and heat-transfer relations. A temperature-dependent rate can make concentration and temperature strongly coupled; assuming constant kkk deliberately excludes that coupling.

The general control-volume energy balance stores internal energy and uses stream enthalpy, heat and work. If full chemical enthalpies include reaction energetics, do not also add a separate reaction-heat term. Here sensible energy and explicit ΔHr\Delta H_rΔHr​ are a consistent alternative.

Worked example

A colder coolant inlet is a disturbance even when it is measured. It changes heat removal, which changes T1T_1T1​, which may change reaction rate and cA1c_{A1}cA1​. A coolant-flow adjustment is a manipulated input because the valve can be commanded.

To close a model of TcoT_{co}Tco​, one cannot merely list that temperature as an independent input. Either apply a quasi-steady coolant balance Qc=wccpc(Tco−Tci)Q_c=w_cc_{pc}(T_{co}-T_{ci})Qc​=wc​cpc​(Tco​−Tci​), with coolant heat capacity cpcc_{pc}cpc​, or include jacket storage and its temperature distribution.

Link to other topics

Reactor modelling provides the balances; process control decides which inputs are available and which outputs matter. Transfer functions will describe the response of those outputs near an operating point.

Conclusion

A useful model begins with a boundary, a variable assignment and enough constitutive relations to determine the states. The labels alone do not close the dynamics.

PDC-04: Mixing tanks and reacting first-order lags

Overview

Assumed: an isothermal CSTR balance and first-order reaction kinetics.

A well-mixed tank converts inlet-composition changes into a first-order lag. Adding reaction changes both the steady gain and the time constant; the hydrodynamic residence time remains V/qV/qV/q.

Intuition

Mixing spreads the arrival of new feed through existing contents. A change is felt immediately, but the old contents are only gradually displaced. Reaction removes A as well as flow removing it, so a concentration deviation disappears faster and a feed increase produces a smaller final concentration increase.

Derivation

Step 1: balance inert solute. With fixed volume VVV, flow qqq, inlet concentration c0c_0c0​ and uniform tank/outlet concentration ccc, assume constant density, no reaction and perfect mixing:

Vc˙=q(c0−c),τc˙+c=c0,τ=V/q.(8)V\dot c=q(c_0-c),\qquad \tau\dot c+c=c_0,\quad \tau=V/q.\tag{8}Vc˙=q(c0​−c),τc˙+c=c0​,τ=V/q.(8)

Reason: fixed volume gives d(Vc)/dt=Vc˙d(Vc)/dt=V\dot cd(Vc)/dt=Vc˙. Dividing by qqq makes the coefficient of ccc equal to one. In the standard first-order form τc˙+c=Kpc0\tau\dot c+c=K_pc_0τc˙+c=Kp​c0​, the derivative coefficient is the time constant and the right-side coefficient is the gain. Setting c˙=0\dot c=0c˙=0 gives c=c0c=c_0c=c0​, so an inert tank has unit gain.

The ratio V/qV/qV/q is also the mean residence time: stored liquid volume divided by volume replaced each second. Perfect mixing allows some new feed to leave quickly and some to remain longer, so it is an average, not an identical transit time for every fluid element.

Step 2: solve a feed step. Initially c=cs=c0sc=c_s=c_{0s}c=cs​=c0s​. For t≥0t\geq0t≥0, the inlet changes permanently by Δc0\Delta c_0Δc0​. Set c′=c−csc'=c-c_sc′=c−cs​; then τc˙′+c′=Δc0\tau\dot c'+c'=\Delta c_0τc˙′+c′=Δc0​ with c′(0)=0c'(0)=0c′(0)=0. Subtracting the old steady balance removes constant terms; because the tank starts there, its initial deviation is zero. First divide the ODE by τ\tauτ, then multiply by et/τe^{t/\tau}et/τ:

ddt(et/τc′)=Δc0τet/τ.\frac{d}{dt}(e^{t/\tau}c')=\frac{\Delta c_0}{\tau}e^{t/\tau}. dtd​(et/τc′)=τΔc0​​et/τ.

Reason: the product rule gives d(et/τc′)/dt=et/τc˙′+et/τc′/τd(e^{t/\tau}c')/dt=e^{t/\tau}\dot c'+e^{t/\tau}c'/\taud(et/τc′)/dt=et/τc˙′+et/τc′/τ, exactly the left side after multiplication. The integrating factor is chosen to create that exact derivative. Integration from zero to ttt gives et/τc′=Δc0(et/τ−1)e^{t/\tau}c'=\Delta c_0(e^{t/\tau}-1)et/τc′=Δc0​(et/τ−1), hence

c′=Δc0(1−e−t/τ).(9)c'=\Delta c_0(1-e^{-t/\tau}).\tag{9}c′=Δc0​(1−e−t/τ).(9)

Step 3: include first-order consumption. For constant rate constant k>0k>0k>0, add loss kVckVckVc:

Vc˙=q(c0−c)−kVc,τ1+kτc˙+c=c01+kτ.(10)V\dot c=q(c_0-c)-kVc, \qquad \frac{\tau}{1+k\tau}\dot c+c=\frac{c_0}{1+k\tau}.\tag{10}Vc˙=q(c0​−c)−kVc,1+kττ​c˙+c=1+kτc0​​.(10)

Reason: reaction consumes kckckc per unit volume, hence kVckVckVc in the whole tank. Collecting terms gives Vc˙+(q+kV)c=qc0V\dot c+(q+kV)c=qc_0Vc˙+(q+kV)c=qc0​. Divide by the coefficient of ccc, namely q+kVq+kVq+kV, to put this in standard form:

τr=Vq+kV=τ1+kτ,Kp=qq+kV=11+kτ.\tau_r=\frac{V}{q+kV}=\frac{\tau}{1+k\tau},\qquad K_p=\frac{q}{q+kV}=\frac{1}{1+k\tau}.τr​=q+kVV​=1+kττ​,Kp​=q+kVq​=1+kτ1​.

The same total removal coefficient appears below both ratios. Storage divided by removal sets the response time; input coefficient divided by removal sets the settled sensitivity. These are different properties even though reaction reduces both here.

Step 4: transform the perturbation balance. The reacting equilibrium is cs=c0s/(1+kτ)c_s=c_{0s}/(1+k\tau)cs​=c0s​/(1+kτ), so it differs from the inert equilibrium. Subtracting it gives τc˙′+(1+kτ)c′=c0′\tau\dot c'+(1+k\tau)c'=c_0'τc˙′+(1+kτ)c′=c0′​. Define cˉ=L[c′]\bar c=\mathcal L[c']cˉ=L[c′] and cˉ0=L[c0′]\bar c_0=\mathcal L[c_0']cˉ0​=L[c0′​], where primes mean deviations from the reacting steady state. With zero initial deviation,

cˉcˉ0=1τs+1+kτ=Kpτrs+1,p=−1+kττ.(11)\frac{\bar c}{\bar c_0}=\frac{1}{\tau s+1+k\tau} =\frac{K_p}{\tau_rs+1},\qquad p=-\frac{1+k\tau}{\tau}.\tag{11}cˉ0​cˉ​=τs+1+kτ1​=τr​s+1Kp​​,p=−τ1+kτ​.(11)

Reason: with zero initial deviation, the transform gives [τs+1+kτ]cˉ=cˉ0[\tau s+1+k\tau]\bar c=\bar c_0[τs+1+kτ]cˉ=cˉ0​. Dividing isolates the output/input ratio. The pole is the value making the denominator zero. Its free-response term is epte^{pt}ept, so a negative pole gives decay, and a more negative pole gives faster decay. Setting s=0s=0s=0 gives G(0)=KpG(0)=K_pG(0)=Kp​, the settled gain for this stable lag.

Motivation and explanation

An excess of A can disappear by washout and by reaction. Both sinks strengthen the restoring effect, shortening the concentration response. At steady state, however, feed A must supply both sinks: qc0=(q+kV)cqc_0=(q+kV)cqc0​=(q+kV)c. Only the fraction q/(q+kV)q/(q+kV)q/(q+kV) leaves unreacted, which explains the smaller concentration gain.

The dimensionless group kτk\taukτ, the Damköhler number for this model, compares the reaction timescale with the flow-through timescale. When kτ≪1k\tau\ll1kτ≪1, washout dominates and Kp→1K_p\to1Kp​→1, τr→τ\tau_r\to\tauτr​→τ. When kτ≫1k\tau\gg1kτ≫1, little A survives, Kp≈1/(kτ)K_p\approx1/(k\tau)Kp​≈1/(kτ), and τr→1/k\tau_r\to1/kτr​→1/k. The fluid's mean residence time is still V/qV/qV/q; reaction shortens the concentration memory without speeding up the liquid flow.

These conclusions require constant q,V,kq,V,kq,V,k and negligible thermal coupling. If flow becomes another changing input, qcqcqc contains a product of changing variables; a local model drops the product of their deviations. A prescribed new constant flow still permits a lag model, but with new coefficients. Temperature-dependent kinetics couples concentration to the energy balance. Second-order consumption kc2kc^2kc2 has local slope 2kcs2kc_s2kcs​, so its linearised response depends on the chosen operating concentration.

Worked example

Let V=2.00V=2.00V=2.00 m3^33, q=0.0200q=0.0200q=0.0200 m3^33 s−1^{-1}−1, so τ=100\tau=100τ=100 s. A feed step of 3.003.003.00 mol m−3^{-3}−3 gives inert-tank deviation c′(100)=1.89636c'(100)=1.89636c′(100)=1.89636 mol m−3^{-3}−3 and final deviation 3.003.003.00 mol m−3^{-3}−3.

With k=0.0100k=0.0100k=0.0100 s−1^{-1}−1, Kp=0.500K_p=0.500Kp​=0.500, τr=50.0\tau_r=50.0τr​=50.0 s and p=−0.0200p=-0.0200p=−0.0200 s−1^{-1}−1. The same feed step gives final deviation 1.501.501.50 mol m−3^{-3}−3 and c′(50)=0.948181c'(50)=0.948181c′(50)=0.948181 mol m−3^{-3}−3.

Both responses reach 63.2121%63.2121\%63.2121% of their own final change at their own time constant. The reacting tank reaches that fraction sooner, but its final increase is only half as large. For a common 95%95\%95% settling criterion, the inert and reacting times are 299.573299.573299.573 s and 149.787149.787149.787 s respectively. Neither response finishes exactly at a finite time. The initial slopes are equal here: Δc0/τ=KpΔc0/τr=0.0300\Delta c_0/\tau=K_p\Delta c_0/\tau_r=0.0300Δc0​/τ=Kp​Δc0​/τr​=0.0300 mol m−3^{-3}−3 s−1^{-1}−1. Reaction changes the subsequent curvature and endpoint, while the unchanged feed step sets the same initial accumulation rate.

Link to other topics

The inert-tank impulse response also describes a CSTR residence-time distribution. The same first-order structure occurs when heat transfer relaxes a sensor toward the bath temperature.

Conclusion

Flow and reaction determine the coefficient of concentration removal. That coefficient controls both the pole and the steady response to feed composition.

PDC-05: Variable-volume tanks and finite pulse balances

Overview

Assumed: perfect mixing and the product rule.

When tank volume changes, balance the stored amount VcVcVc, not concentration alone. A finite-volume pulse is handled by a jump balance before resuming continuous dynamics.

Intuition

Removing well-mixed liquid lowers the amount of solute but does not instantly change its concentration. Adding feed changes both solute amount and liquid volume. Forgetting the volume derivative makes these two actions look incorrectly equivalent.

Derivation

Step 1: track volume and solute. For inlet flow q0q_0q0​, outlet flow qqq, inlet concentration c0c_0c0​, tank concentration ccc and first-order consumption constant kkk, assume constant density and additive volumes:

V˙=q0−q,d(Vc)dt=q0c0−qc−kVc.(12)\dot V=q_0-q,\qquad \frac{d(Vc)}{dt}=q_0c_0-qc-kVc.\tag{12}V˙=q0​−q,dtd(Vc)​=q0​c0​−qc−kVc.(12)

Reason: storage is an extensive amount. Expanding gives Vc˙+cV˙=q0c0−qc−kVcV\dot c+c\dot V=q_0c_0-qc-kVcVc˙+cV˙=q0​c0​−qc−kVc; substitute V˙=q0−q\dot V=q_0-qV˙=q0​−q and cancel −qc-qc−qc:

Vc˙=q0(c0−c)−kVc.(13)V\dot c=q_0(c_0-c)-kVc.\tag{13}Vc˙=q0​(c0​−c)−kVc.(13)

Reason: withdrawal leaves the concentration of remaining well-mixed liquid unchanged directly. It still affects later concentration dynamics through V(t)V(t)V(t).

Step 2: determine the volume history. For specified flows,

V(t)=V(0)+∫0t[q0(θ)−q(θ)] dθ.(14)V(t)=V(0)+\int_0^t[q_0(\theta)-q(\theta)]\,d\theta.\tag{14}V(t)=V(0)+∫0t​[q0​(θ)−q(θ)]dθ.(14)

Reason: integrate the volume balance first, then use the resulting VVV in the concentration ODE. For general time-dependent VVV, this is not a constant-coefficient transfer-function model. If q0=0q_0=0q0​=0 and k=0k=0k=0, the equation gives c˙=0\dot c=0c˙=0 even during withdrawal.

Step 3: cross a short, finite-volume addition. A pulse adds volume VpV_pVp​ at concentration cpc_pcp​. Let (V−,c−)(V_-,c_-)(V−​,c−​) and (V+,c+)(V_+,c_+)(V+​,c+​) denote values immediately before and after it. Neglect reaction and ordinary flow during the short addition:

V+=V−+Vp,V+c+=V−c−+Vpcp,c+=V−c−+VpcpV−+Vp.(15)V_+=V_-+V_p,\qquad V_+c_+=V_-c_-+V_pc_p, \qquad c_+=\frac{V_-c_-+V_pc_p}{V_-+V_p}.\tag{15}V+​=V−​+Vp​,V+​c+​=V−​c−​+Vp​cp​,c+​=V−​+Vp​V−​c−​+Vp​cp​​.(15)

Reason: total volume and solute are conserved across the jump. Use (V+,c+)(V_+,c_+)(V+​,c+​) as initial conditions for the subsequent ODE.

Why does outlet flow disappear from the concentration equation while inlet flow remains? The outlet has exactly the tank composition, so it removes solute and total volume in matching proportions. Feed at c0≠cc_0\ne cc0​=c changes those proportions. As a check, feed at c0=cc_0=cc0​=c cannot change an inert tank's concentration even if it changes the volume. Withdrawal can still shorten the time over which a later feed change acts by reducing the stored volume.

Motivation and explanation

A Dirac impulse idealises an input with finite area and negligible duration. A finite-volume addition also changes the model's holdup; it is not automatically the same experiment as an impulse in feed concentration at fixed volume.

The model stops being valid if the tank drains, overflows, mixes poorly or has appreciable volume change on mixing. A pulse too long to neglect reaction or outlet flow must be integrated with those effects.

Worked example

A tank initially contains V−=1.00V_-=1.00V−​=1.00 m3^33 at c−=2.00c_-=2.00c−​=2.00 mol m−3^{-3}−3. Add Vp=0.100V_p=0.100Vp​=0.100 m3^33 at cp=10.0c_p=10.0cp​=10.0 mol m−3^{-3}−3. The jump balances give V+=1.100V_+=1.100V+​=1.100 m3^33 and c+=2.72727c_+=2.72727c+​=2.72727 mol m−3^{-3}−3.

Treating the addition as extra solute at unchanged volume would overpredict concentration. If the addition instead displaces liquid to keep volume constant, the overflow must appear in the pulse balance.

The new concentration lies between the two original concentrations because it is their volume-weighted average. The added liquid is richer, so concentration rises, but its own volume dilutes the added solute. The jump changes the initial state for the next stage; it is not a new steady state unless later inflow, outflow and reaction also balance there.

Link to other topics

Tank-level control also begins with the volume balance. Linearising flow and concentration products later allows a local transfer-function model around a constant-volume operating point.

Conclusion

Use amount balances through volume changes and jump balances through short additions. The resulting state then determines the next continuous response.

PDC-06: Thermocouple and heated-liquid dynamics

Overview

Assumed: lumped heat capacity and Newton's heat-transfer law.

A temperature sensor and a flowing heated tank both behave as first-order lags, but their time constants have different physical origins. Sensor delay can conceal a process change from feedback.

Intuition

A sensor must gain heat before it reports a hotter bath. Its thermal mass resists a quick change; heat transfer supplies the restoring effect. A flowing tank stores heat too, but replacement by incoming liquid provides its restoring effect in the ideal insulated model.

Derivation

Step 1: balance the sensor. Let sensor mass be mmm, specific heat cpc_pcp​, bath temperature xxx, sensor temperature yyy, heat-transfer coefficient hhh and surface area AhA_hAh​. Assume a uniform sensor temperature, negligible lead conduction, constant properties and a bath unaffected by the sensor:

mcpy˙=hAh(x−y),τmy˙+y=x,τm=mcphAh.(16)mc_p\dot y=hA_h(x-y),\qquad \tau_m\dot y+y=x,\quad \tau_m=\frac{mc_p}{hA_h}.\tag{16}mcp​y˙​=hAh​(x−y),τm​y˙​+y=x,τm​=hAh​mcp​​.(16)

Reason: heat inflow is proportional to bath–sensor temperature difference. Thermal capacity divided by thermal conductance has units of time. Subtract the initial equilibrium and transform:

Gm(s)=yˉxˉ=1τms+1,pm=−1/τm.(17)G_m(s)=\frac{\bar y}{\bar x}=\frac{1}{\tau_ms+1},\qquad p_m=-1/\tau_m.\tag{17}Gm​(s)=xˉyˉ​​=τm​s+11​,pm​=−1/τm​.(17)

Reason: zero initial deviation removes the transform's initial-condition term. The pole represents relaxation of sensor temperature to bath temperature.

Step 2: balance heated liquid. For fixed tank volume VVV, equal flow qqq, density ρ\rhoρ, liquid heat capacity cpLc_{pL}cpL​, feed temperature T0T_0T0​ and heating rate QQQ, assume perfect mixing, constant liquid properties, insulation, no reaction and negligible mixer work:

ρVcpLT˙=ρqcpL(T0−T)+Q,τT˙+T=T0+QρqcpL,τ=V/q.(18)\rho Vc_{pL}\dot T=\rho qc_{pL}(T_0-T)+Q, \qquad \tau\dot T+T=T_0+\frac{Q}{\rho qc_{pL}},\quad \tau=V/q.\tag{18}ρVcpL​T˙=ρqcpL​(T0​−T)+Q,τT˙+T=T0​+ρqcpL​Q​,τ=V/q.(18)

Reason: liquid thermal storage opposes changes driven by feed and heater. For negligible pressure/volume-work effects, liquid internal-energy changes can be approximated by sensible enthalpy changes.

Subtract the steady balance and transform. Holding the other input unchanged gives

GT0(s)=TˉTˉ0=1τs+1,GQ(s)=TˉQˉ=1ρqcpL(τs+1).(19)G_{T_0}(s)=\frac{\bar T}{\bar T_0}=\frac{1}{\tau s+1},\qquad G_Q(s)=\frac{\bar T}{\bar Q}=\frac{1}{\rho qc_{pL}(\tau s+1)}.\tag{19}GT0​​(s)=Tˉ0​Tˉ​=τs+11​,GQ​(s)=Qˉ​Tˉ​=ρqcpL​(τs+1)1​.(19)

Reason: both inputs act on the same stored energy and therefore share the same pole. Their gains differ because temperature and heating rate have different units.

In both models, normalising means dividing by the coefficient of the stored temperature, not by its derivative coefficient. For the sensor this is hAhhA_hhAh​: at equilibrium y=xy=xy=x, so gain is one, and capacity mcpmc_pmcp​ divided by conductance hAhhA_hhAh​ gives the time constant. Increasing sensor mass slows it; increasing exposed area or heat transfer speeds it. The analogy with a mixing tank concerns this balance structure; heat transfer does not imply that sensor material is being replaced by flowing liquid.

For the heated tank, setting the derivative to zero gives T=T0+Q/(ρqcpL)T=T_0+Q/(\rho qc_{pL})T=T0​+Q/(ρqcpL​). A one-kelvin feed change therefore produces a one-kelvin settled tank change, whereas a watt of heating produces 1/(ρqcpL)1/(\rho qc_{pL})1/(ρqcpL​) kelvin. Both inputs share the same relaxation rate because there is only one stored tank temperature. They do not create two separate tank states.

Motivation and explanation

The sensor model needs sufficiently rapid internal heat conduction, often assessed through a small Biot number. A thermowell, fouling or appreciable lead heat loss may add states or change the gain.

The heated-tank time constant equals residence time only under the stated assumptions. Heat loss to surroundings introduces another restoring term; changes in flow change both time constant and heater gain. A negative heater command is not physically available if the actuator only supplies heat.

Worked example

For a sensor with m=0.00200m=0.00200m=0.00200 kg, cp=500c_p=500cp​=500 J kg−1^{-1}−1 K−1^{-1}−1, h=200h=200h=200 W m−2^{-2}−2 K−1^{-1}−1 and Ah=5.00×10−4A_h=5.00\times10^{-4}Ah​=5.00×10−4 m2^22, τm=10.0\tau_m=10.0τm​=10.0 s. Following a bath step from 202020 to 606060 °C, the sensor reads 45.284845.284845.2848 °C after 10.010.010.0 s.

For a 1.001.001.00 m3^33 water tank at q=0.0100q=0.0100q=0.0100 m3^33 s−1^{-1}−1, τ=100\tau=100τ=100 s. With ρ=1000\rho=1000ρ=1000 kg m−3^{-3}−3 and cpL=4200c_{pL}=4200cpL​=4200 J kg−1^{-1}−1 K−1^{-1}−1, a 0.4200.4200.420 MW heating increase gives a final 10.010.010.0 K rise and a 6.321216.321216.32121 K rise after 100100100 s. A sensor lag would delay the measured response further.

The sensor has completed the same fraction of its 404040 K change that the tank has completed of its 101010 K change after one respective time constant. In a measurement chain, tank temperature changes first and supplies a changing input to the sensor. Applying the sensor's step formula directly to that gradual input would misrepresent the combined response; its dynamics must be driven by the actual tank temperature.

Link to other topics

Combining tank and sensor multiplies their transfer functions. This matters for feedback because the controller responds to the measured temperature rather than the true temperature.

Conclusion

Thermal storage divided by a restoring conductance determines each lag. The source of that conductance decides whether its time constant is a heat-transfer time or a flow residence time.

PDC-07: Adiabatic discharge of a gas vessel

Overview

Assumed: ideal-gas properties and the open-system first law.

An insulated gas vessel cools as it discharges. The energy carried away is stream enthalpy, while the energy stored is internal energy; their difference is essential to predicting temperature and pressure.

Intuition

Insulation prevents heat exchange through the wall. It does not prevent energy loss through the outlet. The departing gas carries its internal energy plus flow work, so the remaining gas cools.

Derivation

Step 1: balance mass and energy. Let vessel volume VVV be fixed, stored gas mass mmm, outlet mass flow w>0w>0w>0, uniform temperature TTT and pressure ppp. Assume well-mixed ideal gas with constant specific heats cv,cpc_v,c_pcv​,cp​, no inflow, wall heat storage, heat transfer or shaft work, and negligible outlet kinetic/potential energy. With U=mcvTU=mc_vTU=mcv​T and outlet specific enthalpy H^=cpT\hat H=c_pTH^=cp​T,

m˙=−w,d(mcvT)dt=−wcpT.(20)\dot m=-w,\qquad \frac{d(mc_vT)}{dt}=-wc_pT.\tag{20}m˙=−w,dtd(mcv​T)​=−wcp​T.(20)

Reason: a fixed control volume stores internal energy but stream enthalpy includes flow work at its boundary.

Step 2: eliminate time. Divide the energy balance by cvc_vcv​ and use γ=cp/cv\gamma=c_p/c_vγ=cp​/cv​ and m˙=−w\dot m=-wm˙=−w:

d(mT)dm=γT⇒T+mdTdm=γT⇒dTT=(γ−1)dmm.(21)\frac{d(mT)}{dm}=\gamma T \quad\Rightarrow\quad T+m\frac{dT}{dm}=\gamma T \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{dT}{T}=(\gamma-1)\frac{dm}{m}.\tag{21}dmd(mT)​=γT⇒T+mdmdT​=γT⇒TdT​=(γ−1)mdm​.(21)

Reason: the same mass loss drives both equations, so their ratio removes the unknown discharge-flow law. Integrate from initial (m0,T0)(m_0,T_0)(m0​,T0​):

TT0=(mm0)γ−1.(22)\frac{T}{T_0}=\left(\frac{m}{m_0}\right)^{\gamma-1}.\tag{22}T0​T​=(m0​m​)γ−1.(22)

Step 3: obtain pressure. With mass-specific gas constant R=cp−cvR=c_p-c_vR=cp​−cv​, pV=mRTpV=mRTpV=mRT. Divide by its initial value:

pp0=(mm0)γ,TT0=(pp0)(γ−1)/γ.(23)\frac{p}{p_0}=\left(\frac{m}{m_0}\right)^\gamma, \qquad \frac{T}{T_0}=\left(\frac{p}{p_0}\right)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}.\tag{23}p0​p​=(m0​m​)γ,T0​T​=(p0​p​)(γ−1)/γ.(23)

Reason: fixed volume makes pressure proportional to mTmTmT. The result relates states along discharge, not yet to time.

Step 4: check energy reference invariance. Let specific internal energy instead be U^=cvT+C\hat U=c_vT+CU^=cv​T+C, where CCC is a constant offset. Consistency requires H^=U^+p/ρ=cpT+C\hat H=\hat U+p/\rho=c_pT+CH^=U^+p/ρ=cp​T+C. Then

cvd(mT)dt+Cm˙=−w(cpT+C).c_v\frac{d(mT)}{dt}+C\dot m=-w(c_pT+C). cv​dtd(mT)​+Cm˙=−w(cp​T+C).

Reason: substitute m˙=−w\dot m=-wm˙=−w and the two −wC-wC−wC terms cancel. A changed reference cannot change the temperature prediction. Choosing unrelated enthalpy and internal-energy offsets breaks H^−U^=RT\hat H-\hat U=RTH^−U^=RT.

The product rule exposes the cooling mechanism directly. Expanding the stored energy and using m˙=−w\dot m=-wm˙=−w gives mcvT˙=−w(cp−cv)T=−wRTmc_v\dot T=-w(c_p-c_v)T=-wRTmcv​T˙=−w(cp​−cv​)T=−wRT. Removing mass at unchanged temperature would remove only its internal energy; the outlet enthalpy removes more. That excess is supplied by cooling the remaining gas. Since w>0w>0w>0 and T>0T>0T>0, the predicted temperature derivative is negative.

The outlet law cancels when finding temperature versus remaining mass, so different discharge rates follow the same state relation under these assumptions. They traverse it at different speeds. Although the pressure–temperature exponent resembles a reversible adiabatic closed-system relation, this derivation describes an open vessel losing mass and does not establish that the discharge is reversible.

Motivation and explanation

All temperatures in the ideal-gas and power-law relations are absolute. The relations do not provide m(t)m(t)m(t) without an outlet-flow model. Constant prescribed www gives m=m0−wtm=m_0-wtm=m0​−wt only while gas remains and the prescription is physically sustainable.

The lumped vessel model can fail during rapid discharge with spatial gradients or appreciable wall heat transfer. A nozzle's downstream static temperature need not equal vessel temperature; the outlet enthalpy/kinetic-energy accounting must match the chosen boundary.

Worked example

For T0=300T_0=300T0​=300 K and γ=1.40\gamma=1.40γ=1.40, discharging until m/m0=0.500m/m_0=0.500m/m0​=0.500 gives T=227.357T=227.357T=227.357 K and p/p0=0.378929p/p_0=0.378929p/p0​=0.378929. Pressure falls faster than mass because the remaining gas also cools.

Replacing outlet enthalpy by cvTc_vTcv​T would predict constant vessel temperature under this model, which omits the outlet flow-work contribution.

Link to other topics

The boiler model also distinguishes stored internal energy from stream enthalpy. Thermodynamic reference conventions must remain consistent whenever changing mass multiplies an energy datum.

Conclusion

Insulated open-system discharge is not isothermal. A consistent mass–energy balance gives cooling and pressure decline before any particular discharge-valve law is chosen.

PDC-08: Deviation variables and transfer-function assumptions

Overview

Assumed: basic Laplace-transform rules.

A transfer function describes the forced response of a linear, time-invariant system with zero initial state deviations. Subtracting a steady operating point allows a physically nonzero concentration or temperature to have zero deviation.

Intuition

The baseline is not the disturbance. A tank at a steady concentration already contains material; control asks how much its concentration changes when an input changes. Deviation variables remove the baseline while retaining exactly the perturbation we care about.

Derivation

Step 1: subtract the steady state. For an inert mixed tank, τc˙+c=c0\tau\dot c+c=c_0τc˙+c=c0​. At equilibrium cs=c0sc_s=c_{0s}cs​=c0s​. Define c′=c−csc'=c-c_sc′=c−cs​ and c0′=c0−c0sc_0'=c_0-c_{0s}c0′​=c0​−c0s​. Substitution gives

τc˙′+cs+c′=c0s+c0′⇒τc˙′+c′=c0′.(24)\tau\dot c'+c_s+c'=c_{0s}+c_0' \quad\Rightarrow\quad\tau\dot c'+c'=c_0'.\tag{24}τc˙′+cs​+c′=c0s​+c0′​⇒τc˙′+c′=c0′​.(24)

Reason: the steady values satisfy the original balance and cancel. A prime denotes deviation; a dot denotes time differentiation. They are different operations.

Step 2: transform with the initial condition retained. For any deviation output y′y'y′, write

yˉ(s)=L[y′]=∫0∞y′(t)e−st dt,L[y˙′]=syˉ−y′(0−).(25)\bar y(s)=\mathcal L[y']=\int_0^\infty y'(t)e^{-st}\,dt, \qquad \mathcal L[\dot y']=s\bar y-y'(0^-).\tag{25}yˉ​(s)=L[y′]=∫0∞​y′(t)e−stdt,L[y˙​′]=syˉ​−y′(0−).(25)

Reason: integration by parts produces the initial-value term. The Laplace variable sss has inverse-time units. Transformed variables generally have their original units multiplied by time.

For τy˙′+y′=Kpx′\tau\dot y'+y'=K_px'τy˙​′+y′=Kp​x′,

yˉ=Kpτs+1xˉ+τy′(0−)τs+1.(26)\bar y=\frac{K_p}{\tau s+1}\bar x+ \frac{\tau y'(0^-)}{\tau s+1}.\tag{26}yˉ​=τs+1Kp​​xˉ+τs+1τy′(0−)​.(26)

Reason: collect yˉ\bar yyˉ​ and isolate it. The first term is the input-driven response; the second is the free response to stored initial deviation. Set all initial state deviations to zero to define

G(s)=yˉxˉ∣zero initial state deviations=Kpτs+1.(27)G(s)=\left.\frac{\bar y}{\bar x}\right|_{\text{zero initial state deviations}} =\frac{K_p}{\tau s+1}.\tag{27}G(s)=xˉyˉ​​​zero initial state deviations​=τs+1Kp​​.(27)

Step 3: state the scope. Constant coefficients and superposition define the linear, time-invariant model used here. A SISO transfer function relates one input–output pair. With multiple inputs, hold the other deviations at zero when defining each transfer-matrix element.

Reason: a raw ratio of output to one input with other inputs or initial-state effects present does not isolate that pair's dynamics.

Subtracting a baseline and neglecting an initial condition are separate decisions. Baseline subtraction is an exact change of coordinates. Zero initial deviation is justified only by actually starting at that baseline. If a tank begins above its chosen equilibrium, that stored excess relaxes even when the input deviation stays zero; the second term in equation (26) accounts for it. A transfer function isolates how the imposed input acts, so that free response is handled separately.

For a stable lag, the denominator τs+1\tau s+1τs+1 is the transformed competition between storage and removal. The transform has made a differential equation algebraic; it has not added a new physical mechanism. Returning to the time domain gives the same exponential relaxation derived by an integrating factor.

Motivation and explanation

Subtraction gives zero initial deviations only when the process actually starts at the chosen equilibrium. If it starts elsewhere, include the free-response term. For a second-order ODE, both output and derivative initial conditions matter.

Zero initial state does not require a step input to have zero value or derivative immediately after t=0t=0t=0. A step deliberately jumps. Taking t=0t=0t=0 at the disturbance is a convenient origin, not a special physical assumption. A nonlinear model only gains a local transfer function after linearisation.

Worked example

An inert tank initially has cs=c0s=5.00c_s=c_{0s}=5.00cs​=c0s​=5.00 kmol m−3^{-3}−3. Its feed steps to 8.008.008.00 kmol m−3^{-3}−3. The transformed input deviation is cˉ0=3.00/s\bar c_0=3.00/scˉ0​=3.00/s, not 8.00/s8.00/s8.00/s, and the initial output deviation is zero.

For τ=100\tau=100τ=100 s,

cˉ=3.00s(100s+1),c(t)=5.00+3.00(1−e−t/100).\bar c=\frac{3.00}{s(100s+1)},\qquad c(t)=5.00+3.00(1-e^{-t/100}). cˉ=s(100s+1)3.00​,c(t)=5.00+3.00(1−e−t/100).

The absolute concentration after 100100100 s is 6.896366.896366.89636 kmol m−3^{-3}−3. The same transfer function would apply around any inert-tank baseline at unchanged flow and volume.

Link to other topics

Deviation variables support both first-order response analysis and Taylor linearisation. A pole belongs to the process transfer function; additional factors in an input transform belong to the imposed signal.

Conclusion

A transfer function separates process dynamics from baseline, initial conditions and input waveform. Preserve that distinction when interpreting its poles and gain.

PDC-09: First-order step and impulse responses

Overview

Assumed: the transfer function of a self-regulating mixed or thermal tank.

For G(s)=Kp/(τs+1)G(s)=K_p/(\tau s+1)G(s)=Kp​/(τs+1) with τ>0\tau>0τ>0, gain sets the final response and time constant sets the speed. Step and impulse experiments expose different features of the same stored-state dynamics.

Intuition

A persistent step keeps supplying a new condition until the tank settles. A brief pulse supplies a finite perturbation and then leaves the tank to relax. The response to the pulse therefore decays, while the step response accumulates that decaying response.

Derivation

Step 1: apply a step. Let H(t)H(t)H(t) be the unit Heaviside step and x′=ΔxH(t)x'=\Delta x H(t)x′=ΔxH(t). For zero initial state, xˉ=Δx/s\bar x=\Delta x/sxˉ=Δx/s, so

yˉ=KpΔxs(τs+1)=KpΔx[1s−1s+1/τ].(28)\bar y=\frac{K_p\Delta x}{s(\tau s+1)} =K_p\Delta x\left[\frac1s-\frac{1}{s+1/\tau}\right].\tag{28}yˉ​=s(τs+1)Kp​Δx​=Kp​Δx[s1​−s+1/τ1​].(28)

Reason: multiply the proposed partial fractions by s(τs+1)s(\tau s+1)s(τs+1) to check that their numerator is one. Invert each term:

y′(t)=KpΔx(1−e−t/τ),y˙′(t)=KpΔxτe−t/τ.(29)y'(t)=K_p\Delta x(1-e^{-t/\tau}),\quad \dot y'(t)=\frac{K_p\Delta x}{\tau}e^{-t/\tau}.\tag{29}y′(t)=Kp​Δx(1−e−t/τ),y˙​′(t)=τKp​Δx​e−t/τ.(29)

Reason: the pole −1/τ-1/\tau−1/τ generates a decaying exponential; the input's 1/s1/s1/s generates the constant final term.

Step 2: interpret the time constant. At t=τt=\taut=τ, the normalised response is 1−e−11-e^{-1}1−e−1. The initial tangent is y′≈(KpΔx/τ)ty'\approx (K_p\Delta x/\tau)ty′≈(Kp​Δx/τ)t, which meets the final response at t=τt=\taut=τ. To reach fraction fff of the final change, solve f=1−e−t/τf=1-e^{-t/\tau}f=1−e−t/τ:

tf=−τln⁡(1−f),0<f<1.(30)t_f=-\tau\ln(1-f),\qquad 0<f<1.\tag{30}tf​=−τln(1−f),0<f<1.(30)

Reason: the remaining distance is an exponentially decaying fraction.

Step 3: apply an impulse. Let δ(t)\delta(t)δ(t) be a unit-area Dirac impulse, with L[δ]=1\mathcal L[\delta]=1L[δ]=1. It is a distribution, not an ordinary finite-height signal. For impulse area IxI_xIx​, x′=Ixδ(t)x'=I_x\delta(t)x′=Ix​δ(t) and

yˉ=IxG(s),y′(t)=KpIxτe−t/τ(t≥0).(31)\bar y=I_xG(s),\qquad y'(t)=\frac{K_pI_x}{\tau}e^{-t/\tau}\quad(t\geq0).\tag{31}yˉ​=Ix​G(s),y′(t)=τKp​Ix​​e−t/τ(t≥0).(31)

Reason: invert the single first-order pole. Since δ\deltaδ has inverse-time units, IxI_xIx​ has input units times time. Integrating the ODE across the impulse gives τ[y′(0+)−y′(0−)]=KpIx\tau[y'(0^+)-y'(0^-)]=K_pI_xτ[y′(0+)−y′(0−)]=Kp​Ix​, confirming the output jump.

The distance still to travel is KpΔx−y′=KpΔx e−t/τK_p\Delta x-y'=K_p\Delta x\,e^{-t/\tau}Kp​Δx−y′=Kp​Δxe−t/τ. In each time interval of length τ\tauτ, this remaining distance is multiplied by e−1e^{-1}e−1; the response never uses up a fixed amount per second. That is why the rise is initially steep and then flattens. The initial tangent reaches the final level at τ\tauτ only if its starting slope were maintained; the actual slope immediately starts falling.

An impulse has a different endpoint because its forcing ends. Its finite area changes the stored state across the brief input, then the unforced state decays back to baseline. A step continually supports a displaced equilibrium. Their different final values reflect different experiments, not different process gains.

Motivation and explanation

A lag begins responding immediately; its delayed approach is not dead time. Negative KpK_pKp​ reverses the response direction but does not change stability when τ>0\tau>0τ>0. Comparing the magnitude of gain with one makes sense only after accounting for units or using a consistent scaling.

The unit-step derivative is the unit-impulse response for this zero-state LTI system. Its impulse-response area is KpK_pKp​. Real pulses approximate the impulse only when their duration is short relative to the dynamics and they do not appreciably change the process parameters.

Worked example

With Kp=2.00K_p=2.00Kp​=2.00, τ=20.0\tau=20.0τ=20.0 s and step Δx=3.00\Delta x=3.00Δx=3.00 in input units, the final output change is 6.006.006.00 and y′(20)=3.79272y'(20)=3.79272y′(20)=3.79272 in output units. For a unit-area input pulse, y′(20)=0.0367879y'(20)=0.0367879y′(20)=0.0367879 in the corresponding output units.

A first-order response reaches 63.2121%63.2121\%63.2121% of its final change at one time constant, 95.0213%95.0213\%95.0213% at three and 99.3262%99.3262\%99.3262% at five. For τ=100\tau=100τ=100 s, the exact time to 95%95\%95% is 299.573299.573299.573 s.

For comparison, at two time constants the step has completed 86.4665%86.4665\%86.4665% of its final change. All these fractions refer to the output change from its initial value, not to its absolute value. Dividing by KpΔxK_p\Delta xKp​Δx removes amplitude and units, leaving one common curve against t/τt/\taut/τ for every stable first-order lag without delay.

Link to other topics

An integrator responds to a step with continuing accumulation instead of settling. Cascading several lags changes the early response and creates higher-order dynamics.

Conclusion

The step measures steady sensitivity and relaxation speed; the impulse isolates the decaying response to a finite input area.

PDC-10: Integrators and transport dead time

Overview

Assumed: volume balances and the time-shift rule for Laplace transforms.

Two elementary process elements behave very differently from a self-regulating lag. An integrator stores a persistent imbalance; ideal transport dead time shifts a signal without smoothing it.

Intuition

A tank with a fixed pumped outlet cannot increase outflow automatically when its level rises. Extra inflow keeps accumulating. A plug-flow pipe instead carries a temperature front downstream: nothing arrives until its transit time has elapsed, then the same front appears.

Derivation

Step 1: derive the integrator from level. For a tank of constant cross-sectional area AAA, level hhh, inlet q0q_0q0​ and prescribed pumped outlet qqq, assume both flows are independent of hhh:

Ah˙=q0−q,Ah˙′=q0′−q′,hˉ=1As(qˉ0−qˉ).(32)A\dot h=q_0-q,\qquad A\dot h'=q_0'-q',\qquad \bar h=\frac{1}{As}(\bar q_0-\bar q).\tag{32}Ah˙=q0​−q,Ah˙′=q0′​−q′,hˉ=As1​(qˉ​0​−qˉ​).(32)

Reason: volume is AhAhAh; subtract the balanced baseline and transform with zero initial level deviation. With net-flow deviation x′=q0′−q′x'=q_0'-q'x′=q0′​−q′, the transfer function is 1/(As)1/(As)1/(As), with pole at zero. A constant imbalance Δq\Delta qΔq gives h′=Δq t/Ah'=\Delta q\,t/Ah′=Δqt/A; an impulse of net volume IVI_VIV​ gives a persistent level jump IV/AI_V/AIV​/A.

A scaled form is THy˙′=x′T_H\dot y'=x'TH​y˙​′=x′ and G=1/(THs)G=1/(T_Hs)G=1/(TH​s). Here THT_HTH​ is a holdup time when x′,y′x',y'x′,y′ are defined with compatible normalised units; AAA in the dimensional level equation is an area, not a time.

Step 2: derive transport delay. For pipe length LLL, uniform constant velocity uuu, negligible axial mixing and heat exchange, a fluid element takes td=L/ut_d=L/utd​=L/u to reach the outlet. With inlet temperature deviation x′x'x′ and outlet y′y'y′, zero deviation history before the disturbance gives

y′(t)={0,t<td,x′(t−td),t≥td.(33)y'(t)=\begin{cases}0,&t<t_d,\\x'(t-t_d),&t\geq t_d.\end{cases}\tag{33}y′(t)={0,x′(t−td​),​t<td​,t≥td​.​(33)

Reason: each outlet parcel carries its inlet condition from one transit time earlier. Substitute θ=t−td\theta=t-t_dθ=t−td​ into the transform:

yˉ=∫td∞x′(t−td)e−st dt=e−std∫0∞x′(θ)e−sθ dθ,Gd(s)=e−std.(34)\bar y=\int_{t_d}^{\infty}x'(t-t_d)e^{-st}\,dt =e^{-st_d}\int_0^{\infty}x'(\theta)e^{-s\theta}\,d\theta, \qquad G_d(s)=e^{-st_d}.\tag{34}yˉ​=∫td​∞​x′(t−td​)e−stdt=e−std​∫0∞​x′(θ)e−sθdθ,Gd​(s)=e−std​.(34)

Reason: the exponential factor accounts for the time shift and does not change the signal's eventual amplitude.

The missing term in the level balance is a level-dependent removal term. A lag would have a contribution proportional to −h′-h'−h′ that grows as level rises and eventually cancels the changed inflow. Here the prescribed pump removes the same flow at every level, so no new level restores the balance. When the extra inflow ends, the level stops rising but retains its accumulated offset. This is the physical memory represented by 1/s1/s1/s.

A delay stores a history of conditions travelling along a pipe. It does not continuously blend that history into a single mixed state. For a step, compare the shapes: a lag begins immediately and curves toward a final value; an integrator ramps while the imbalance persists; an ideal delay stays unchanged and then jumps. Increasing tdt_dtd​ shifts the arrival time without reducing step amplitude or rounding the front.

Motivation and explanation

The integrator is not bounded-input bounded-output (BIBO) stable: a bounded nonzero constant input creates an unbounded ramp. Its zero-input level deviation remains constant, so it is neutrally stable in that state sense rather than an exponentially growing mode. It is not asymptotically stable or self-regulating. Real level is bounded by emptying or overflowing, where the ideal model stops applying.

A pure delay is BIBO stable and has unit steady gain. It is not a finite-order rational transfer function. A first-order lag begins changing immediately; a pure delay waits and then reproduces the input. Axial dispersion, wall heat exchange or velocity variation makes a real pipe more than a pure delay.

Worked example

For A=2.00A=2.00A=2.00 m2^22 and persistent net inflow 0.002000.002000.00200 m3^33 s−1^{-1}−1, level rises at 0.001000.001000.00100 m s−1^{-1}−1 and increases by 0.06000.06000.0600 m in 60.060.060.0 s.

For a 20.020.020.0 m pipe of diameter 0.04000.04000.0400 m carrying 0.001000.001000.00100 m3^33 s−1^{-1}−1, cross-sectional velocity is 0.7957750.7957750.795775 m s−1^{-1}−1 and transit time is 25.132725.132725.1327 s. An ideal inlet temperature step reaches the outlet after that time with its original amplitude.

Link to other topics

A gravity-draining tank introduces a level-dependent outflow and can become self-regulating. Transport delay matters in controller design because measurements may describe a condition created well before the current actuator command.

Conclusion

A pole at zero represents accumulation without restoring action. The exponential delay factor represents travel time, not a slow approach to equilibrium.

PDC-11: Second-order models, poles and damping regimes

Overview

Assumed: two coupled first-order balances and exponential solutions of linear ODEs.

Second-order behaviour requires two dynamic states or one second-order equation. Its pole pair determines whether deviations relax monotonically, decay while oscillating, persist, or grow.

Intuition

Two tanks smooth a disturbance twice. A mass and spring exchange kinetic and elastic energy and can overshoot. Both have two states, but the mechanism of coupling decides whether oscillation is possible.

Derivation

Step 1: eliminate an intermediate tank state. Let x′x'x′ be inlet deviation, y′y'y′ the first-tank outlet and z′z'z′ the second, with positive time constants τ1,τ2\tau_1,\tau_2τ1​,τ2​ and unity gains:

τ1y˙′+y′=x′,τ2z˙′+z′=y′.\tau_1\dot y'+y'=x',\qquad \tau_2\dot z'+z'=y'. τ1​y˙​′+y′=x′,τ2​z˙′+z′=y′.

Reason: each mixed-tank balance relaxes its state toward the upstream condition. Substitute y′=τ2z˙′+z′y'=\tau_2\dot z'+z'y′=τ2​z˙′+z′ and its derivative into the first balance:

τ1τ2z¨′+(τ1+τ2)z˙′+z′=x′.(35)\tau_1\tau_2\ddot z'+(\tau_1+\tau_2)\dot z'+z'=x'.\tag{35}τ1​τ2​z¨′+(τ1​+τ2​)z˙′+z′=x′.(35)

Step 2: define the standard form. For a general ODE a2y¨′+a1y˙′+a0y′=bx′a_2\ddot y'+a_1\dot y'+a_0y'=bx'a2​y¨​′+a1​y˙​′+a0​y′=bx′ with constant coefficients and a0≠0a_0\ne0a0​=0, the conventional form applies when a2/a0>0a_2/a_0>0a2​/a0​>0:

τ2y¨′+2ζτy˙′+y′=Kpx′,τ2=a2/a0,2ζτ=a1/a0,Kp=b/a0.(36)\tau^2\ddot y'+2\zeta\tau\dot y'+y'=K_px',\quad \tau^2=a_2/a_0,\quad 2\zeta\tau=a_1/a_0,\quad K_p=b/a_0.\tag{36}τ2y¨​′+2ζτy˙​′+y′=Kp​x′,τ2=a2​/a0​,2ζτ=a1​/a0​,Kp​=b/a0​.(36)

Reason: divide by a0a_0a0​ and define τ>0\tau>0τ>0 as the second-order time scale and ζ\zetaζ as the dimensionless damping factor. For a forced mass–spring system my¨′+μy˙′+ky′=F′m\ddot y'+\mu\dot y'+ky'=F'my¨​′+μy˙​′+ky′=F′, τ=m/k\tau=\sqrt{m/k}τ=m/k​, ζ=μ/(2mk)\zeta=\mu/(2\sqrt{mk})ζ=μ/(2mk​) and force-to-displacement gain is 1/k1/k1/k. Weight has already cancelled when displacement is measured from equilibrium.

Step 3: transform and find the poles. Zero initial state and derivative give

G(s)=Kpτ2s2+2ζτs+1,p1,2=−ζ±ζ2−1τ.(37)G(s)=\frac{K_p}{\tau^2s^2+2\zeta\tau s+1},\qquad p_{1,2}=\frac{-\zeta\pm\sqrt{\zeta^2-1}}{\tau}.\tag{37}G(s)=τ2s2+2ζτs+1Kp​​,p1,2​=τ−ζ±ζ2−1​​.(37)

Reason: solve the quadratic characteristic equation; each root multiplies time in a free-response exponential.

Damping Pole pattern Response of this constant-numerator model
ζ>1\zeta>1ζ>1 Two negative real poles Overdamped; monotonic stable step
ζ=1\zeta=1ζ=1 Repeated pole −1/τ-1/\tau−1/τ Critically damped
0<ζ<10<\zeta<10<ζ<1 Complex pair with negative real part Decaying oscillations
ζ=0\zeta=0ζ=0 Pair ±i/τ\pm i/\tau±i/τ Undamped; persistent free oscillations
ζ<0\zeta<0ζ<0 Poles with positive real part Growing deviations

Reason: the real part controls decay/growth and the imaginary part supplies oscillation frequency. At ζ=−1\zeta=-1ζ=−1, the repeated positive pole also gives instability.

Normalising by a0a_0a0​ makes the final output/input ratio visible as Kp=b/a0K_p=b/a_0Kp​=b/a0​; matching the derivative coefficients then defines τ\tauτ and ζ\zetaζ. Do not read a1a_1a1​ alone as a first-order time constant: both derivative terms jointly determine two poles. For a complex pair, e(−ζ/τ+iωd)te^{(-\zeta/\tau+i\omega_d)t}e(−ζ/τ+iωd​)t separates into decay envelope e−ζt/τe^{-\zeta t/\tau}e−ζt/τ and oscillation. The envelope time is τ/ζ\tau/\zetaτ/ζ, while the oscillation period depends on ωd\omega_dωd​.

For the mass–spring analogy, displacement can keep increasing after crossing equilibrium because velocity is still positive: kinetic energy carries it past the target. Dissipation reduces that stored energy on each swing. Two sequential mixing tanks lack this inertial exchange mechanism; the downstream tank merely follows a progressively changing upstream input. The shared second-order equation does not make their physical couplings identical.

Motivation and explanation

The natural angular frequency is ωn=1/τ\omega_n=1/\tauωn​=1/τ, in rad per unit time. The undamped period is 2πτ2\pi\tau2πτ; τ\tauτ itself is not an oscillation period.

For two passive lags, τ=τ1τ2\tau=\sqrt{\tau_1\tau_2}τ=τ1​τ2​​ and ζ=(τ1+τ2)/(2τ1τ2)≥1\zeta=(\tau_1+\tau_2)/(2\sqrt{\tau_1\tau_2})\geq1ζ=(τ1​+τ2​)/(2τ1​τ2​​)≥1, because (τ1−τ2)2≥0(\sqrt{\tau_1}-\sqrt{\tau_2})^2\geq0(τ1​​−τ2​​)2≥0. Thus a simple cascade of two positive lags cannot be underdamped. Equal lags are critically damped. Undamped poles are not BIBO stable, even though their free oscillations are bounded.

Worked example

The graph uses t/τt/\taut/τ horizontally and output normalised by its unit-step gain vertically. For two tanks with τ1=20.0\tau_1=20.0τ1​=20.0 s and τ2=80.0\tau_2=80.0τ2​=80.0 s, the combined time scale is 40.040.040.0 s and ζ=1.25\zeta=1.25ζ=1.25. The poles are −0.0500-0.0500−0.0500 and −0.0125-0.0125−0.0125 s−1^{-1}−1: both modes decay without oscillation.

For τ=10.0\tau=10.0τ=10.0 s and ζ=0.500\zeta=0.500ζ=0.500, poles are −0.0500±0.0866025i-0.0500\pm0.0866025i−0.0500±0.0866025i s−1^{-1}−1. The response oscillates with a decaying envelope rather than behaving like the two passive tanks.

Read the response graph in two parts: the common final normalised value expresses gain, while the curvature and crossings express damping. For the unequal tanks, the pole nearer zero, −0.0125-0.0125−0.0125 s−1^{-1}−1, corresponds to the slower 80.080.080.0 s mode and governs the late tail when its coefficient is nonzero. For the complex example, the real part sets how quickly peaks shrink and the imaginary part sets how closely they are spaced.

Link to other topics

Pole analysis generalises to higher-order models. Overshoot and decay ratio translate this second-order pole pair into directly observable response features.

Conclusion

Second order describes the number of dynamic states; damping describes how their modes behave. The physical coupling determines which damping regimes are possible.

PDC-12: Second-order step response, overshoot and decay ratio

Overview

Assumed: the standard second-order model with constant numerator, no zeros or dead time, and zero initial output and derivative.

Deriving the step response makes overshoot, oscillation period and decay ratio consequences of the pole pair. These relations apply to the standard model, not every process with two poles.

Intuition

The steady response is a constant particular solution. The transient is the free mode needed to match the starting state. In an underdamped process, that free mode repeatedly crosses the final value while losing amplitude.

Derivation

Step 1: separate steady and transient parts. Let the input step be Δx\Delta xΔx and normalise r(t)=y′(t)/(KpΔx)r(t)=y'(t)/(K_p\Delta x)r(t)=y′(t)/(Kp​Δx), with nonzero KpΔxK_p\Delta xKp​Δx. Then τ2r¨+2ζτr˙+r=1\tau^2\ddot r+2\zeta\tau\dot r+r=1τ2r¨+2ζτr˙+r=1. For distinct poles, write r=1+C1ep1t+C2ep2tr=1+C_1e^{p_1t}+C_2e^{p_2t}r=1+C1​ep1​t+C2​ep2​t. Initial conditions require

C1+C2=−1,p1C1+p2C2=0.C_1+C_2=-1,\qquad p_1C_1+p_2C_2=0. C1​+C2​=−1,p1​C1​+p2​C2​=0.

Reason: neither output nor its first derivative can jump under a finite step for this strictly proper second-order model. Solving these two equations gives

r=1+p2ep1t−p1ep2tp1−p2.(38)r=1+\frac{p_2e^{p_1t}-p_1e^{p_2t}}{p_1-p_2}.\tag{38}r=1+p1​−p2​p2​ep1​t−p1​ep2​t​.(38)

Step 2: handle the repeated root. At ζ=1\zeta=1ζ=1, p=−1/τp=-1/\taup=−1/τ and the transient has form (C1+C2t)e−t/τ(C_1+C_2t)e^{-t/\tau}(C1​+C2​t)e−t/τ. Enforcing r(0)=r˙(0)=0r(0)=\dot r(0)=0r(0)=r˙(0)=0 gives C1=−1C_1=-1C1​=−1, C2=−1/τC_2=-1/\tauC2​=−1/τ, so

r=1−(1+t/τ)e−t/τ.(39)r=1-(1+t/\tau)e^{-t/\tau}.\tag{39}r=1−(1+t/τ)e−t/τ.(39)

Reason: repeated roots need a polynomial factor; simply setting the two exponential coefficients equal would lose one independent solution.

Step 3: use complex poles. For 0<ζ<10<\zeta<10<ζ<1, define a=ζ/τa=\zeta/\taua=ζ/τ and ωd=1−ζ2/τ\omega_d=\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}/\tauωd​=1−ζ2​/τ. Write r=1+e−at(Ccos⁡ωdt+Dsin⁡ωdt)r=1+e^{-at}(C\cos\omega_dt+D\sin\omega_dt)r=1+e−at(Ccosωd​t+Dsinωd​t). The same initial conditions give C=−1C=-1C=−1 and D=−a/ωdD=-a/\omega_dD=−a/ωd​, hence

r=1−e−ζt/τ[cos⁡(ωdt)+ζ1−ζ2sin⁡(ωdt)].(40)r=1-e^{-\zeta t/\tau}\left[\cos(\omega_dt)+ \frac{\zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}\sin(\omega_dt)\right].\tag{40}r=1−e−ζt/τ[cos(ωd​t)+1−ζ2​ζ​sin(ωd​t)].(40)

Reason: conjugate modes combine into a real damped sinusoid.

Step 4: locate the first peak. Differentiate the preceding result; cosine terms cancel:

r˙=e−ζt/ττ1−ζ2sin⁡(ωdt).\dot r=\frac{e^{-\zeta t/\tau}}{\tau\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}\sin(\omega_dt). r˙=τ1−ζ2​e−ζt/τ​sin(ωd​t).

Reason: extrema occur at zero sine. The first peak is at tp=π/ωdt_p=\pi/\omega_dtp​=π/ωd​, where cosine is −1-1−1. If B=∣KpΔx∣B=|K_p\Delta x|B=∣Kp​Δx∣ is the total steady change and AAA is the first peak's excess magnitude above the final value,

AB=exp⁡[−πζ1−ζ2],tp=πτ1−ζ2.(41)\frac AB=\exp\left[-\frac{\pi\zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}\right],\qquad t_p=\frac{\pi\tau}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}.\tag{41}BA​=exp[−1−ζ2​πζ​],tp​=1−ζ2​πτ​.(41)

Step 5: compare successive peaks on the same side. They are separated by T=2π/ωdT=2\pi/\omega_dT=2π/ωd​. If CCC is the next same-side peak's excess magnitude, its envelope has fallen by e−aTe^{-aT}e−aT:

CA=exp⁡[−2πζ1−ζ2]=(AB)2,T=2πτ1−ζ2.(42)\frac CA=\exp\left[-\frac{2\pi\zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}\right] =\left(\frac AB\right)^2,\qquad T=\frac{2\pi\tau}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}.\tag{42}AC​=exp[−1−ζ2​2πζ​]=(BA​)2,T=1−ζ2​2πτ​.(42)

Reason: compare peaks measured relative to the final value, not their absolute heights. Consecutive extrema on opposite sides are only half a period apart.

The constant 111 in the normalised solution is the forced equilibrium. The transient starts at −1-1−1 to cancel it at t=0t=0t=0 and must also match the zero initial slope. This is why the oscillatory part is not an arbitrary sine curve placed around the endpoint: its sine and cosine weights are fixed by the starting state. As ttt grows, the transient decays and leaves the forced equilibrium.

At the first peak the response has travelled half an oscillation period. There the sine term is zero and the cosine is −1-1−1, so the excess above the final value equals the exponential decay factor at that instant. Successive peaks on the same side are a full period apart, so their excesses shrink by the full-period decay factor. In the figure, measure excesses from the final-value line; measuring peak heights from zero would mix the steady part into the transient ratio.

Motivation and explanation

The horizontal reference through the oscillations represents the final value; BBB spans the initial-to-final change. For negative gain, reflect the response and use magnitudes in the overshoot ratio.

Taking ζ→0\zeta\rightarrow0ζ→0 gives r=1−cos⁡(t/τ)r=1-\cos(t/\tau)r=1−cos(t/τ), with no final settled value. Taking ζ→1\zeta\rightarrow1ζ→1 requires the repeated-root limit rather than substituting into a singular-looking expression. Zeros or delays alter measured response shape and invalidate a blind fit of these formulas.

Worked example

For τ=10.0\tau=10.0τ=10.0 s and ζ=0.500\zeta=0.500ζ=0.500, ωd=0.0866025\omega_d=0.0866025ωd​=0.0866025 rad s−1^{-1}−1, tp=36.2760t_p=36.2760tp​=36.2760 s and T=72.5520T=72.5520T=72.5520 s. Overshoot is A/B=0.163034A/B=0.163034A/B=0.163034, or 16.3034%16.3034\%16.3034%, and same-side decay ratio is C/A=0.0265799C/A=0.0265799C/A=0.0265799. A unit-gain unit-step response therefore first peaks at 1.163031.163031.16303.

For critical damping, the normalised response at t=τt=\taut=τ is 1−2e−1=0.2642411-2e^{-1}=0.2642411−2e−1=0.264241. Unlike a first-order lag, it has zero initial slope.

The 16.3034%16.3034\%16.3034% overshoot means the first peak exceeds the final change by that fraction; it does not mean the output peaks at 0.1630340.1630340.163034. The same-side ratio 0.02657990.02657990.0265799 means the next excess is only that fraction of the first excess. The repeated-lag response's zero initial slope also explains its smaller progress at t=τt=\taut=τ: the second tank must wait for the first tank to develop a temperature difference, even though there is no exact waiting interval.

Link to other topics

Observed oscillation can reveal a complex pole pair. Cascaded tank examples illustrate the critically damped formula without requiring a mechanical analogy.

Conclusion

Overshoot comes from the transient mode carrying the output past its steady value. Pole decay and frequency determine the excess peak and the spacing between peaks.

PDC-13: Series blocks and the pipe–two-tank response

Overview

Assumed: a plug-flow delay and perfectly mixed tank energy balances.

A pipe followed by two insulated tanks combines transport delay with two first-order lags. Multiplying blocks preserves each element's physical role and produces a delayed second-order response.

Intuition

The pipe postpones the arrival of a hot front. The first tank dilutes it into stored liquid; the second smooths that already changing temperature. The outlet stays unchanged until the front arrives, then initially changes very gently.

Derivation

Step 1: construct each element. For pipe length LLL, diameter DDD, constant volumetric flow qqq and uniform velocity u=4q/(πD2)u=4q/(\pi D^2)u=4q/(πD2), the delay is td=L/ut_d=L/utd​=L/u. Let temperatures along the sequence be T0,T1,T2,T3T_0,T_1,T_2,T_3T0​,T1​,T2​,T3​, and tank volumes be V2,V3V_2,V_3V2​,V3​.

For ideal plug flow, Tˉ1=e−tdsTˉ0\bar T_1=e^{-t_ds}\bar T_0Tˉ1​=e−td​sTˉ0​. With constant liquid properties and no heat losses, each tank balance is ρVicpT˙i=ρqcp(Ti−1−Ti)\rho V_ic_p\dot T_i=\rho qc_p(T_{i-1}-T_i)ρVi​cp​T˙i​=ρqcp​(Ti−1​−Ti​), so its deviation transfer function is 1/(τis+1)1/(\tau_is+1)1/(τi​s+1), τi=Vi/q\tau_i=V_i/qτi​=Vi​/q.

Reason: the pipe preserves the input waveform after transit, whereas tank storage gives a lag.

Step 2: substitute through the series. For blocks G1,G2,G3G_1,G_2,G_3G1​,G2​,G3​, Tˉ1=G1Tˉ0\bar T_1=G_1\bar T_0Tˉ1​=G1​Tˉ0​, Tˉ2=G2Tˉ1\bar T_2=G_2\bar T_1Tˉ2​=G2​Tˉ1​, Tˉ3=G3Tˉ2\bar T_3=G_3\bar T_2Tˉ3​=G3​Tˉ2​. Therefore

Tˉ3Tˉ0=e−tds(τ2s+1)(τ3s+1).(43)\frac{\bar T_3}{\bar T_0}=\frac{e^{-t_ds}}{(\tau_2s+1)(\tau_3s+1)}.\tag{43}Tˉ0​Tˉ3​​=(τ2​s+1)(τ3​s+1)e−td​s​.(43)

Reason: the output of one element is the next element's input; repeated substitution multiplies their SISO transfer functions.

Step 3: invert equal lags. For τ2=τ3=τ\tau_2=\tau_3=\tauτ2​=τ3​=τ and inlet step ΔT0\Delta T_0ΔT0​, first remove the delay and decompose

1s(τs+1)2=1s−ττs+1−τ(τs+1)2.\frac{1}{s(\tau s+1)^2} =\frac1s-\frac{\tau}{\tau s+1}-\frac{\tau}{(\tau s+1)^2}. s(τs+1)21​=s1​−τs+1τ​−(τs+1)2τ​.

Reason: multiplying by the common denominator verifies the coefficients. The inverse transforms of the last two terms are e−t/τe^{-t/\tau}e−t/τ and (t/τ)e−t/τ(t/\tau)e^{-t/\tau}(t/τ)e−t/τ. Restore the delay by shifting the complete causal response:

T3′(t)={0,t<td,ΔT0[1−(1+t−tdτ)e−(t−td)/τ],t≥td.(44)T_3'(t)=\begin{cases} 0,&t<t_d,\\ \Delta T_0\left[1-\left(1+\frac{t-t_d}{\tau}\right)e^{-(t-t_d)/\tau}\right],&t\geq t_d. \end{cases}\tag{44}T3′​(t)={0,ΔT0​[1−(1+τt−td​​)e−(t−td​)/τ],​t<td​,t≥td​.​(44)

Reason: the pipe postpones the entire two-tank response. The rational part has a repeated pole −1/τ-1/\tau−1/τ and is critically damped.

The delay and lags answer different questions. The delay says when the response can first appear. The two tank states say how it develops after that arrival. Immediately after arrival, tank 1 starts warming, but tank 2 still has almost no inlet–contents temperature difference, so its initial slope is zero. For every positive elapsed time after arrival the outlet does change; the initially flat tangent does not add another interval of dead time.

Multiplying the zero-frequency gains gives one: with no heat loss, every element ultimately reaches the new inlet temperature. The repeated pole supplies the te−t/τt e^{-t/\tau}te−t/τ term, which changes the rise shape without changing that endpoint. Shift both occurrences of time in the causal response when reinstating the pipe delay; shifting only the exponential would violate the starting conditions.

Motivation and explanation

Scalar LTI series multiplication commutes, so reordering these ideal blocks leaves the overall input–output transfer function unchanged. Their intermediate signals do change. Reordering real equipment may also change heat losses, mixing, flows or the relevant model; the algebra does not establish physical interchangeability.

Two lags produce a zero initial slope after the delay. They create a smooth rise, not extra exact dead time. The final gain remains one because the insulated system eventually passes the changed temperature through unchanged.

Worked example

Let q=1.00×10−3q=1.00\times10^{-3}q=1.00×10−3 m3^33 s−1^{-1}−1, D=0.0400D=0.0400D=0.0400 m, L=20.0L=20.0L=20.0 m and V2=V3=0.100V_2=V_3=0.100V2​=V3​=0.100 m3^33. The calculated velocity is 0.7957750.7957750.795775 m s−1^{-1}−1, td=25.1327t_d=25.1327td​=25.1327 s and both time constants are 100100100 s. Thus

G(s)=e−25.1327s(100s+1)2.G(s)=\frac{e^{-25.1327s}}{(100s+1)^2}. G(s)=(100s+1)2e−25.1327s​.

For a 1.001.001.00 K inlet step, T3′(125)=0.263753T_3'(125)=0.263753T3′​(125)=0.263753 K. Rounding the transit time to 252525 s is reasonable for a coarse estimate, but the calculation here retains the value from the specified geometry.

Link to other topics

Series-block algebra extends to sensor and actuator lags. Parallel paths instead require signed addition of contributions to an output.

Conclusion

Build the overall response from physically derived elements. The delay sets its onset; the repeated tank pole sets its subsequent smooth approach.

PDC-14: Summing contributions and duplicating signals

Overview

Assumed: superposition in linear deviation models.

Series elements multiply; independent contributions to the same output add with their signs. A signal branch copies information and does not divide its value like a material-flow splitter.

Intuition

In a heated tank, warmer feed and extra heater power both affect temperature. Each input passes through its own response path, then the temperature contributions combine. Measuring that temperature does not consume part of it.

Derivation

Step 1: begin with the balance. For fixed V,q,ρ,cpV,q,\rho,c_pV,q,ρ,cp​, no heat loss or reaction, set τ=V/q\tau=V/qτ=V/q and Cf=ρqcpC_f=\rho qc_pCf​=ρqcp​, the flowing heat-capacity rate. The tank deviation equation is

τT˙′+T′=T0′+Q′/Cf.(45)\tau\dot T'+T'=T_0'+Q'/C_f.\tag{45}τT˙′+T′=T0′​+Q′/Cf​.(45)

Reason: subtract the steady energy balance so the two forcing contributions remain. Transform with zero initial deviation:

Tˉ=G1Tˉ0+G2Qˉ,G1=1τs+1,G2=1Cf(τs+1).(46)\bar T=G_1\bar T_0+G_2\bar Q,\qquad G_1=\frac1{\tau s+1},\quad G_2=\frac1{C_f(\tau s+1)}.\tag{46}Tˉ=G1​Tˉ0​+G2​Qˉ​,G1​=τs+11​,G2​=Cf​(τs+1)1​.(46)

Reason: both sources feed the same state, but the heater input must first be converted from power to temperature-equivalent forcing.

Step 2: apply a signed summing junction. A junction labelled +++ on one path and −-− on another forms yˉ=yˉ1−yˉ2\bar y=\bar y_1-\bar y_2yˉ​=yˉ​1​−yˉ​2​. If both paths start with the same input xˉ\bar xxˉ, their equivalent block is G1−G2G_1-G_2G1​−G2​; two positive paths give G1+G2G_1+G_2G1​+G2​.

Reason: superposition is addition of output effects, including their signs. Signals summed at a junction must have compatible units; raw temperature and power cannot be added.

Step 3: duplicate a signal. If one ideal branch sends Tˉ\bar TTˉ onward and another to a sensor, both pre-sensor branches equal Tˉ\bar TTˉ. The measured signal is Tˉm=GmTˉ\bar T_m=G_m\bar TTˉm​=Gm​Tˉ, where GmG_mGm​ is the sensor transfer function.

Reason: a branch copies a numerical variable. It is not a material balance and does not halve temperature. Sensor dynamics or loading, if relevant, must be represented separately.

It is legitimate to sum the two temperature contributions because each is already expressed in output-temperature units. The factor 1/Cf1/C_f1/Cf​ converts heating power into the feed-temperature change with the same thermal effect. Then the common lag applies to their sum. A block diagram is bookkeeping for these equations: a line is a signal, a summing point adds signed effects, and a branch sends the same value to more than one destination.

Exact dynamic compensation requires the paths to cancel as functions of sss, not merely at s=0s=0s=0. If the heater has an extra actuator lag, its final temperature contribution can still cancel the cold feed while its early contribution is too slow. That produces a temporary temperature drop even when the eventual temperature error is zero.

Motivation and explanation

Superposition holds for the linear model at fixed coefficients. If flow changes, the heater gain and time constant change too; products such as q′T′q'T'q′T′ require linearisation before this simple summation is justified.

For an ideal measurement scale, Gm(0)=1G_m(0)=1Gm​(0)=1, but a sensor may still lag. Treating the measured output as instantly equal to the true output hides a pole in the feedback path.

Worked example

For water with Cf=42000C_f=42000Cf​=42000 W K−1^{-1}−1 and τ=100\tau=100τ=100 s, let the feed temperature fall by 5.005.005.00 K while heating rises by 210000210000210000 W. Their step contributions sum to

T′(t)=[−5.00+21000042000](1−e−t/100)=0.T'(t)=\left[-5.00+\frac{210000}{42000}\right](1-e^{-t/100})=0. T′(t)=[−5.00+42000210000​](1−e−t/100)=0.

The exact cancellation follows because both paths share the same tank lag in this model and the commands occur together. An actuator lag in the heat path, a delayed disturbance measurement, or inaccurate CfC_fCf​ produces a transient error even when the steady effects cancel.

Link to other topics

Feedforward exploits signed summation to oppose disturbance effects. Transfer-function matrices organise the same idea when several inputs affect several outputs.

Conclusion

Write the signal equations before simplifying a block diagram. Their units, signs and branch meanings prevent most combination errors.
