PDC-15: Transfer-function matrices and coupled CSTR concentrations

Overview

Assumed: constant-volume, isothermal CSTR balances for A→BA\rightarrow BA→B.

A MIMO model is a matrix of input–output responses. The reacting CSTR shows how an input can affect its own species directly and another species through a reaction pathway.

Intuition

More A in the feed raises reactor A and therefore makes more B. More B in the feed raises B without creating A because the reaction is irreversible. The matrix should express this directional coupling, not artificially give every input the same effect.

Derivation

Step 1: define the matrix convention. With nnn input deviations and mmm output deviations,

yˉ=G(s)xˉ,yˉi=∑j=1nGij(s)xˉj.(47)\bar{\boldsymbol y}=\boldsymbol G(s)\bar{\boldsymbol x},\qquad \bar y_i=\sum_{j=1}^nG_{ij}(s)\bar x_j.\tag{47}yˉ​=G(s)xˉ,yˉ​i​=j=1∑n​Gij​(s)xˉj​.(47)

Reason: output row iii sums the contributions from input columns jjj. Define each GijG_{ij}Gij​ with all other input deviations and initial state deviations zero. Each entry has units of its row's output divided by its column's input.

Step 2: balance both components. Let VVV be volume, qqq equal inlet/outlet flow, τ=V/q\tau=V/qτ=V/q, k>0k>0k>0 first-order rate constant, cA0,cB0c_{A0},c_{B0}cA0​,cB0​ feed concentrations and cA,cBc_A,c_BcA​,cB​ tank concentrations. Assume constant density, one mole B formed per mole A consumed, no volume change and perfect mixing:

τc˙A+(1+kτ)cA=cA0,τc˙B+cB=cB0+kτcA.(48)\tau\dot c_A+(1+k\tau)c_A=c_{A0},\qquad \tau\dot c_B+c_B=c_{B0}+k\tau c_A.\tag{48}τc˙A​+(1+kτ)cA​=cA0​,τc˙B​+cB​=cB0​+kτcA​.(48)

Reason: A reaction loss is an equal B reaction source. Subtract the steady balances and transform:

cˉA=cˉA0τs+1+kτ,cˉB=cˉB0τs+1+kτcˉA0(τs+1)(τs+1+kτ).\bar c_A=\frac{\bar c_{A0}}{\tau s+1+k\tau},\qquad \bar c_B=\frac{\bar c_{B0}}{\tau s+1}+ \frac{k\tau\bar c_{A0}}{(\tau s+1)(\tau s+1+k\tau)}. cˉA​=τs+1+kτcˉA0​​,cˉB​=τs+1cˉB0​​+(τs+1)(τs+1+kτ)kτcˉA0​​.

Reason: solve the A equation first, then substitute it into the B equation. This produces

[cˉAcˉB]=[1τs+1+kτ0kτ(τs+1)(τs+1+kτ)1τs+1][cˉA0cˉB0].(49)\begin{bmatrix}\bar c_A\\\bar c_B\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac1{\tau s+1+k\tau}&0\\ \dfrac{k\tau}{(\tau s+1)(\tau s+1+k\tau)}&\dfrac1{\tau s+1} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}\bar c_{A0}\\\bar c_{B0}\end{bmatrix}.\tag{49}[cˉA​cˉB​​]=​τs+1+kτ1​(τs+1)(τs+1+kτ)kτ​​0τs+11​​​[cˉA0​cˉB0​​].(49)

Step 3: check the conserved total. Add the two ODEs:

τd(cA+cB)dt+(cA+cB)=cA0+cB0.(50)\tau\frac{d(c_A+c_B)}{dt}+(c_A+c_B)=c_{A0}+c_{B0}.\tag{50}τdtd(cA​+cB​)​+(cA​+cB​)=cA0​+cB0​.(50)

Reason: reaction cancels in the total concentration balance. Equivalently, the A-feed column sums to 1/(τs+1)1/(\tau s+1)1/(τs+1), because

1τs+1+kτ+kτ(τs+1)(τs+1+kτ)=1τs+1.\frac1{\tau s+1+k\tau}+\frac{k\tau}{(\tau s+1)(\tau s+1+k\tau)}=\frac1{\tau s+1}. τs+1+kτ1​+(τs+1)(τs+1+kτ)kτ​=τs+11​.

Read the first column as one experiment: change feed A, hold feed B unchanged, and observe both outputs. The upper entry is direct survival of A; the lower entry is production of B through the changing A inventory. Read the second column as a different experiment: feed B changes without changing A. The zero in the upper-right entry records the absence of a reverse reaction or other coupling under these assumptions.

Adding the two output rows checks more than the final numbers. Reaction redistributes molecules between A and B but cannot alter their total in this one-to-one conversion. The total therefore follows the inert-tank mode at all times. A faster A-removal mode is compatible with a slower total-concentration mode because consuming A creates B rather than removing total A plus B.

Motivation and explanation

The two dynamic modes have poles −(1+kτ)/τ-(1+k\tau)/\tau−(1+kτ)/τ and −1/τ-1/\tau−1/τ. The B response to feed A contains both modes: A first changes, then its changed conversion supplies B. The A response to feed B is zero under the stated irreversible, uncoupled chemistry.

This is a MIMO concentration model. The heated tank with two inputs but only one temperature output is MISO, a single-output special case. If temperature affects kkk, or multiple reactions occur, the zero entry and pole structure can change.

Worked example

Take τ=100\tau=100τ=100 s and k=0.0100k=0.0100k=0.0100 s−1^{-1}−1. A unit step in cA0c_{A0}cA0​ with no cB0c_{B0}cB0​ change gives

cA′=12(1−e−2t/100),cB′=12−e−t/100+12e−2t/100.c_A'=\tfrac12(1-e^{-2t/100}),\qquad c_B'=\tfrac12-e^{-t/100}+\tfrac12e^{-2t/100}. cA′​=21​(1−e−2t/100),cB′​=21​−e−t/100+21​e−2t/100.

These follow by taking the A response and subtracting it from total response 1−e−t/1001-e^{-t/100}1−e−t/100. At 100100100 s, cA′=0.432332c_A'=0.432332cA′​=0.432332 and cB′=0.199788c_B'=0.199788cB′​=0.199788 in the concentration unit used for the input. Final deviations are 0.5000.5000.500 each. Their sum tracks an inert-tank concentration response at every time.

The final half-and-half split is about the extra feed A: half survives as A and half appears as B. Early on, A begins rising immediately, while B initially has zero slope because its extra production rate first needs extra A to build up. Thus the equal final gains do not imply equal transient curves.

Link to other topics

Material conservation is a strong check on a coupled model. The boiler matrix will combine two different balances and include an integrating inventory output.

Conclusion

Rows identify outputs and columns identify inputs. Coupling entries should follow actual pathways, and conserved combinations provide independent verification.

PDC-16: Boiler mass–energy balance and integrating inventory

Overview

Assumed: saturated-phase properties, a rigid control volume and simultaneous linear equations.

For a boiler held at fixed pressure, mass and energy balances determine liquid-inventory dynamics and steam production together. This idealised model contains an integrator for inventory and algebraic feed/heat effects on steam flow.

Intuition

Extra heat evaporates stored liquid unless the feed rises to replace it. Extra subcooled feed can temporarily reduce steam output because some heat must warm that feed. Pressure is assumed already maintained; its dynamic control is outside this reduced model.

Derivation

Step 1: define properties and storage. Let FFF be liquid-feed mass flow, GGG steam mass flow, QHQ_HQH​ heat input, VL,VGV_L,V_GVL​,VG​ liquid/vapour volumes, and VT=VL+VGV_T=V_L+V_GVT​=VL​+VG​ fixed vessel volume. Hold pressure at 888 bar absolute, so saturation temperature is 170.4170.4170.4 °C and phase properties remain constant. Densities are ρL,ρG\rho_L,\rho_GρL​,ρG​; specific internal energies are U^L,U^G\hat U_L,\hat U_GU^L​,U^G​; feed and steam specific enthalpies are H^F,H^G\hat H_F,\hat H_GH^F​,H^G​. Ignore heat loss and other work.

Mass is M=ρLVL+ρG(VT−VL)M=\rho_LV_L+\rho_G(V_T-V_L)M=ρL​VL​+ρG​(VT​−VL​). Internal energy is U=ρLU^LVL+ρGU^G(VT−VL)U=\rho_L\hat U_LV_L+\rho_G\hat U_G(V_T-V_L)U=ρL​U^L​VL​+ρG​U^G​(VT​−VL​). Differentiate at fixed properties:

(ρL−ρG)V˙L=F−G,(ρLU^L−ρGU^G)V˙L=FH^F−GH^G+QH.(51)(\rho_L-\rho_G)\dot V_L=F-G,\qquad (\rho_L\hat U_L-\rho_G\hat U_G)\dot V_L =F\hat H_F-G\hat H_G+Q_H.\tag{51}(ρL​−ρG​)V˙L​=F−G,(ρL​U^L​−ρG​U^G​)V˙L​=FH^F​−GH^G​+QH​.(51)

Reason: total vessel volume is constant, so increasing liquid volume displaces vapour volume. Enthalpy accounts for energy carried by streams; internal energy describes storage.

Step 2: eliminate steam flow. Define Dρ=ρL−ρGD_\rho=\rho_L-\rho_GDρ​=ρL​−ρG​ and DU=ρLU^L−ρGU^GD_U=\rho_L\hat U_L-\rho_G\hat U_GDU​=ρL​U^L​−ρG​U^G​. From mass, G=F−DρV˙LG=F-D_\rho\dot V_LG=F−Dρ​V˙L​. Substitute into energy:

DUV˙L=F(H^F−H^G)+DρH^GV˙L+QH.D_U\dot V_L=F(\hat H_F-\hat H_G)+D_\rho\hat H_G\dot V_L+Q_H. DU​V˙L​=F(H^F​−H^G​)+Dρ​H^G​V˙L​+QH​.

Reason: use one balance to close the unknown flow in the other. Define

B=DρH^G−DU=ρL(H^G−U^L)−ρG(H^G−U^G).B=D_\rho\hat H_G-D_U =\rho_L(\hat H_G-\hat U_L)-\rho_G(\hat H_G-\hat U_G). B=Dρ​H^G​−DU​=ρL​(H^G​−U^L​)−ρG​(H^G​−U^G​).

Then

V˙L=aF+bQH,G=cF+dQH,a=H^G−H^FB, b=−1B, c=1−Dρa, d=DρB.(52)\dot V_L=aF+bQ_H,\quad G=cF+dQ_H, \quad a=\frac{\hat H_G-\hat H_F}{B},\ b=-\frac1B, \ c=1-D_\rho a,\ d=\frac{D_\rho}{B}.\tag{52}V˙L​=aF+bQH​,G=cF+dQH​,a=BH^G​−H^F​​, b=−B1​, c=1−Dρ​a, d=BDρ​​.(52)

Reason: isolate V˙L\dot V_LV˙L​, then recover GGG from mass. With zero initial deviation, subtract the steady balances and transform:

[VˉLGˉ]=[a/sb/scd][FˉQˉH].(53)\begin{bmatrix}\bar V_L\\\bar G\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}a/s&b/s\\c&d\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}\bar F\\\bar Q_H\end{bmatrix}.\tag{53}[VˉL​Gˉ​]=[a/sc​b/sd​][FˉQˉ​H​​].(53)

Reason: liquid volume is the integral of its rate; steam flow is algebraic in this reduced model.

The signs follow the energy pathways. At fixed feed, extra heat evaporates liquid, so the heat-to-liquid-volume coefficient bbb is negative and the heat-to-steam coefficient ddd is positive. At fixed heat, extra subcooled feed requires warming, so it accumulates as liquid and can reduce steam production. A feed-to-steam coefficient slightly below zero is therefore compatible with mass conservation: the changed inventory absorbs more mass than the feed increase alone.

There is no VLV_LVL​ term on the right of V˙L=aF+bQH\dot V_L=aF+bQ_HV˙L​=aF+bQH​. Consequently, a persistent nonzero aF′+bQH′aF'+bQ_H'aF′+bQH′​ cannot be removed merely by reaching a different level. The integrator represents that continuing accumulation. Steam flow has no separate stored state in this fixed-pressure approximation; the algebraic balance assigns it an immediate change. Real pressure and heat-transfer dynamics would resolve that idealisation into additional dynamics.

Motivation and explanation

The inventory pole is at zero: at fixed F,QHF,Q_HF,QH​ the model provides no level-dependent restoring effect. A persistent mismatch drains or fills the boiler until the assumed phase inventory no longer exists. The algebraic steam-flow row represents direct feedthrough, not a lag with an extremely short measured time constant.

At steady state Gs=FsG_s=F_sGs​=Fs​ and QHs=Fs(H^G−H^F)Q_{Hs}=F_s(\hat H_G-\hat H_F)QHs​=Fs​(H^G​−H^F​). The model deliberately omits pressure dynamics, finite evaporation kinetics and heat storage in equipment. It is valid only while saturated liquid and vapour coexist and the fixed-pressure approximation is adequate.

Use H^F=675.5\hat H_F=675.5H^F​=675.5, H^G=2768.3\hat H_G=2768.3H^G​=2768.3, U^L=720.0\hat U_L=720.0U^L​=720.0, U^G=2576.0\hat U_G=2576.0U^G​=2576.0 kJ kg−1^{-1}−1, and ρL=896.9\rho_L=896.9ρL​=896.9, ρG=4.2\rho_G=4.2ρG​=4.2 kg m−3^{-3}−3. [VˉL​Gˉ​]≈[1.13968×10−3/s−0.0173881​−5.44570×10−7/s4.86137×10−4​][FˉQˉ​H​​].

Here sss is in s−1^{-1}−1. At fixed heat, a 1.001.001.00 kg s−1^{-1}−1 feed increase gives V˙L′=1.13968×10−3\dot V_L'=1.13968\times10^{-3}V˙L′​=1.13968×10−3 m3^33 s−1^{-1}−1 and G′=−0.0173881G'=-0.0173881G′=−0.0173881 kg s−1^{-1}−1. Inventory control restores a stable level when a process naturally integrates. The boiler also shows why proper transfer functions can contain direct input-to-output terms.

PDC-17: Poles, repeated modes and stability

Overview

Assumed: partial fractions and complex exponentials.

Poles describe the free dynamic modes visible in an input–output model. Repeated poles add polynomial factors; complex conjugate poles combine into real oscillations. Stability must be defined carefully at poles on the imaginary axis.

Intuition

After a pulse is over, each dynamic mode retains a memory of the perturbation. A negative real part makes that memory fade. A positive real part amplifies it. Zero real part does not supply decay, even when a particular free response stays bounded.

Derivation

Step 1: identify process poles. For a rational SISO model G(s)=N(s)/D(s)G(s)=N(s)/D(s)G(s)=N(s)/D(s) in reduced form, poles are roots of D(s)D(s)D(s) and zeros are roots of N(s)N(s)N(s). In yˉ=G(s)xˉ\bar y=G(s)\bar xyˉ​=G(s)xˉ, extra roots supplied by xˉ\bar xxˉ are input-signal poles, not additional process states.

Step 2: invert elementary pole terms. For a pole ppp and integer j≥1j\geq1j≥1,

L−1[Cj(s−p)j]=Cjtj−1(j−1)!ept.(54)\mathcal L^{-1}\left[\frac{C_j}{(s-p)^j}\right] =C_j\frac{t^{j-1}}{(j-1)!}e^{pt}.\tag{54}L−1[(s−p)jCj​​]=Cj​(j−1)!tj−1​ept.(54)

Reason: L[ept]=1/(s−p)\mathcal L[e^{pt}]=1/(s-p)L[ept]=1/(s−p) and successive powers of ttt arise by differentiating with respect to sss. Repeated poles therefore require all powers from 1/(s−p)1/(s-p)1/(s−p) through 1/(s−p)j1/(s-p)^j1/(s−p)j in the partial fraction expansion.

Step 3: combine a complex pair. Let p=a+ibp=a+ibp=a+ib, residue C=α+iβC=\alpha+i\betaC=α+iβ, and conjugate terms p∗,C∗p^*,C^*p∗,C∗, where i2=−1i^2=-1i2=−1. Euler's formula gives

Cept+C∗ep∗t=2eat[αcos⁡(bt)−βsin⁡(bt)].(55)Ce^{pt}+C^*e^{p^*t} =2e^{at}[\alpha\cos(bt)-\beta\sin(bt)].\tag{55}Cept+C∗ep∗t=2eat[αcos(bt)−βsin(bt)].(55)

Reason: imaginary terms cancel because a real physical model has conjugate poles and residues. The envelope is controlled by aaa, and frequency by ∣b∣|b|∣b∣.

Step 4: relate modes to stability. For a finite-dimensional proper rational model with no unstable hidden modes, strictly negative real parts imply asymptotic decay and BIBO stability. A right-half-plane pole gives instability. Simple imaginary-axis poles give nondecaying free modes but fail BIBO stability; bounded resonant forcing can accumulate indefinitely. Repeated imaginary-axis poles can grow even without forcing.

Reason: multiplying a decaying exponential by any finite-degree polynomial still tends to zero; without exponential decay that guarantee disappears.

For a simple real pole, moving farther left increases the decay rate because epte^{pt}ept falls more quickly. A complex pair adds repeated sign changes while its real part still controls the envelope. Repeating a negative pole adds a factor such as ttt, so a mode can initially grow in magnitude before decaying; the exponential ultimately wins. A repeated pole at zero instead gives powers of time with no decaying exponential to suppress them.

Among observable stable modes with nonzero weights, poles nearest the imaginary axis usually govern the late tail. Their weights still matter: a slow mode with a very small coefficient may be barely visible over the time interval of interest. Pole locations predict possible rates and frequencies, while the particular input, output and numerator determine how much each mode appears.

Motivation and explanation

Cancellation can hide a mode from one input–output transfer function. An exact unstable pole–zero cancellation is not evidence of internal stability: an initial condition or another input/output path may expose the hidden growing state. Use the full state model when making that claim.

For physical rational models, properness requires numerator degree no larger than denominator degree. Equal degrees allow direct feedthrough. Strictly proper models have lower numerator degree. Pure transport delay is causal but non-rational, so the polynomial-degree test does not describe it.

Worked example

Consider the dimensional time coordinate in seconds and the transfer function

G(s)=1s6+2s5+14s4+60s3+81s2+34s=1s(s+1)2(s+2)[(s−1)2+16].G(s)=\frac1{s^6+2s^5+14s^4+60s^3+81s^2+34s} =\frac1{s(s+1)^2(s+2)[(s-1)^2+16]}. G(s)=s6+2s5+14s4+60s3+81s2+34s1​=s(s+1)2(s+2)[(s−1)2+16]1​.

The poles are 000, −1-1−1 twice, −2-2−2 and 1±4i1\pm4i1±4i, in s−1^{-1}−1. The positive-real-part pair makes the system unstable.

For a unit-area impulse, partial fractions give the response for t≥0t\geq0t≥0:

y′(t)=134−e−2t50−e−t100−te−t20+et[cos⁡(4t)−0.25sin⁡(4t)]1700.y'(t)=\frac1{34}-\frac{e^{-2t}}{50}-\frac{e^{-t}}{100} -\frac{te^{-t}}{20} +\frac{e^t[\cos(4t)-0.25\sin(4t)]}{1700}. y′(t)=341​−50e−2t​−100e−t​−20te−t​+1700et[cos(4t)−0.25sin(4t)]​.

The constant comes from the process pole at zero because the input is an impulse. The te−tte^{-t}te−t term reveals the repeated pole, and the growing oscillation reveals 1±4i1\pm4i1±4i. The residues and factorisation can be checked by recombining the rational terms before inversion.

The growing oscillation may start with a small coefficient, but its ete^tet envelope eventually overwhelms the decaying terms and constant. A short observation that looks quiet cannot overturn the positive-real-part pole test. Here the constant term comes from a process integrator; in a stable lag's step response, a constant can instead come from the step's input pole. Keeping the experiment specified avoids confusing those cases.

Link to other topics

Pole locations determine whether the final-value theorem can be used. Zeros influence the weighting of these modes and can cause an initial response opposite to the final change.

Conclusion

Interpret each pole as a mode with a decay rate and, when complex, an oscillation frequency. Distinguish visible input–output stability from stability of all internal states.

PDC-18: Zeros, direct feedthrough and inverse response

Overview

Assumed: poles and partial-fraction responses.

Zeros reshape the forced response without creating a new exponential mode. A right-half-plane zero can make the output initially move opposite to its final direction, even when every process pole is stable.

Intuition

Two physical pathways can compete. A fast pathway may initially push the output down while a slower but stronger pathway eventually raises it. Their sum can therefore dip before rising; the zero encodes that competition.

Derivation

Step 1: separate modes from their weights. Write a strictly proper model with distinct poles as G(s)=∑jCj/(s−pj)G(s)=\sum_j C_j/(s-p_j)G(s)=∑j​Cj​/(s−pj​). For each pole,

Cj=lim⁡s→pj(s−pj)G(s).(56)C_j=\lim_{s\to p_j}(s-p_j)G(s).\tag{56}Cj​=s→pj​lim​(s−pj​)G(s).(56)

Reason: multiplying removes that term's simple singularity; all other terms vanish in the limit. Changing the numerator changes residues CjC_jCj​, hence the relative amplitudes of modes, while unreduced denominator roots stay fixed unless cancellation occurs.

Step 2: build an inverse-response example. Add two stable first-order pathways:

G(s)=4s+1−6s+2=2(1−s)(s+1)(s+2).(57)G(s)=\frac4{s+1}-\frac6{s+2} =\frac{2(1-s)}{(s+1)(s+2)}.\tag{57}G(s)=s+14​−s+26​=(s+1)(s+2)2(1−s)​.(57)

Reason: put the contributions over a common denominator. Poles are −1,−2-1,-2−1,−2 and the zero is +1+1+1. Both modes decay, but the zero is in the right half-plane. For a unit step,

yˉ=G(s)s=1s−4s+1+3s+2,y′=1−4e−t+3e−2t.(58)\bar y=\frac{G(s)}s=\frac1s-\frac4{s+1}+\frac3{s+2}, \qquad y'=1-4e^{-t}+3e^{-2t}.\tag{58}yˉ​=sG(s)​=s1​−s+14​+s+23​,y′=1−4e−t+3e−2t.(58)

Reason: invert each partial fraction. At zero, y′=0y'=0y′=0 but y˙′=4−6=−2\dot y'=4-6=-2y˙​′=4−6=−2; the final value is 111. The initial direction opposes the final direction.

Step 3: distinguish feedthrough from storage. If numerator and denominator degrees are equal, long division gives G(s)=D0+Gsp(s)G(s)=D_0+G_{sp}(s)G(s)=D0​+Gsp​(s), where D0D_0D0​ is a constant and GspG_{sp}Gsp​ is strictly proper. In the time domain, y′=D0x′y'=D_0x'y′=D0​x′ plus the stored-state response.

Reason: a constant block passes an input directly and may create an immediate output jump under a step. It need not be unphysical: the reduced boiler steam-flow model has this form.

The two pathways settle to different strengths: their gains are 444 and −3-3−3, so the positive contribution wins at long times. Initially, their slopes are 444 and −6-6−6, so the faster negative path wins. That change of dominance explains the dip without requiring an unstable pole. The zero at +1+1+1 appears when the two pathway expressions are combined; it describes their cancellation in the transfer numerator, not an extra growing state.

Feedthrough is another distinct feature. With a finite step and strictly proper lag pathways, the state output remains continuous and only its slope changes. A nonzero direct term D0D_0D0​ adds an immediate jump D0ΔxD_0\Delta xD0​Δx on top of the stored-state response. Such a jump, a gradual inverse response, and a transport waiting time therefore have different mathematical and physical causes.

Motivation and explanation

A right-half-plane zero does not by itself make the open-loop transfer function unstable. It constrains response shaping and makes exact stable causal inversion problematic. A numerator zero can cancel a denominator pole in a mathematical expression, but that can hide internal dynamics.

Not every stable two-pole model has the monotonic step response of the standard constant-numerator second-order model. Its zero structure and feedthrough matter too. The example assumes linearity and no transport delay.

Worked example

For the two-pathway model, solve y˙′=4e−t−6e−2t=0\dot y'=4e^{-t}-6e^{-2t}=0y˙​′=4e−t−6e−2t=0. This gives the minimum at t=ln⁡(3/2)=0.405465t=\ln(3/2)=0.405465t=ln(3/2)=0.405465 s, where y′=−1/3=−0.333333y'=-1/3=-0.333333y′=−1/3=−0.333333. The response eventually approaches +1+1+1.

Physically, the negative pathway has the faster pole −2-2−2 and initially contributes slope −6-6−6; the positive pathway contributes slope +4+4+4. Their final step contributions are −3-3−3 and +4+4+4, leaving a positive total.

Link to other topics

The final-value theorem predicts the endpoint but cannot reveal inverse response. Controller design must account for both poles and zeros when interpreting the transient.

Conclusion

Poles set the available modes; zeros set how the input excites them. A stable process can still have an initially misleading response direction.

PDC-19: Steady-state gain and the final-value theorem

Overview

Assumed: Laplace transforms of step inputs.

Steady-state gain is the change in settled output per change in settled input. Evaluating G(0)G(0)G(0) gives this gain only when the relevant response actually settles; an algebraic limit alone cannot prove that it does.

Intuition

A constant input eventually leaves only a constant balance if all transient modes decay. Gain is the sensitivity of that remaining balance. If a mode grows or keeps oscillating, there is no settled output to interpret.

Derivation

Step 1: read the gain from a balance. For τy˙′+y′=Kpx′\tau\dot y'+y'=K_px'τy˙​′+y′=Kp​x′, a final constant input Δx\Delta xΔx and settled output Δy\Delta yΔy satisfy Δy=KpΔx\Delta y=K_p\Delta xΔy=Kp​Δx.

Reason: a steady state has zero derivative. Gain has output/input units; it need not be dimensionless.

Step 2: use the transform. The final-value theorem states, under its validity conditions,

lim⁡t→∞y′(t)=lim⁡s→0syˉ(s).(59)\lim_{t\to\infty}y'(t)=\lim_{s\to0}s\bar y(s).\tag{59}t→∞lim​y′(t)=s→0lim​syˉ​(s).(59)

For a proper rational signal transform, a standard sufficient condition is that all poles of syˉs\bar ysyˉ​ lie strictly in the left half-plane after cancellations. Equivalently, yˉ\bar yyˉ​ may have a simple pole at the origin for a constant final value, but no other nondecaying modes. A finite causal delay preserves a settling signal's endpoint.

Reason: the theorem requires decay of every nonconstant term. Check the complete output transform, including the imposed input and any initial-state contribution, rather than only one process denominator.

Step 3: specialise to a step. For zero-state yˉ=G(s)Δx/s\bar y=G(s)\Delta x/syˉ​=G(s)Δx/s,

Δy=Δxlim⁡s→0G(s),Kp=G(0),(60)\Delta y=\Delta x\lim_{s\to0}G(s),\qquad K_p=G(0),\tag{60}Δy=Δxs→0lim​G(s),Kp​=G(0),(60)

provided the step response settles and the limit is finite.

Reason: the step's 1/s1/s1/s factor cancels the theorem's factor sss. For a stable MIMO model, applying a step in one input at a time gives the gain matrix G(0)\boldsymbol G(0)G(0). Integrating output paths generally lack a finite steady gain.

Evaluating at s=0s=0s=0 removes derivative factors, which is why it reproduces the static balance when a static balance is actually reached. The final-value theorem makes that connection precise; it does not supply decay that the process lacks. A unit step has transform 1/s1/s1/s, so syˉ=G(s)s\bar y=G(s)syˉ​=G(s) for that experiment, and the stability condition must be checked before taking its limit.

Gain and speed can change independently. Multiplying a stable transfer function by a constant scales its endpoint without moving its poles. Adding pure delay shifts its timing without changing G(0)G(0)G(0). Moving a pole while adjusting the numerator can change speed at fixed gain. A final-value calculation deliberately discards transient detail and must be paired with a dynamics check when timing matters.

Motivation and explanation

A lag's pole comes from the process; a simple 1/s1/s1/s in the output transform may merely come from a step input. Confusing them would label a settling step response unstable.

A pure transport delay satisfies e−tds→1e^{-t_ds}\rightarrow1e−td​s→1 at s=0s=0s=0. It changes timing but not steady gain. In an unstable model, a finite G(0)G(0)G(0) does not establish an attainable endpoint.

Worked example

Take

G(s)=10e−5s(s+1)(s+5)(s+10),x′(t)=1−e−t/10,xˉ=1s(10s+1).G(s)=\frac{10e^{-5s}}{(s+1)(s+5)(s+10)},\qquad x'(t)=1-e^{-t/10},\quad \bar x=\frac1{s(10s+1)}. G(s)=(s+1)(s+5)(s+10)10e−5s​,x′(t)=1−e−t/10,xˉ=s(10s+1)1​.

The nonconstant modes have negative poles −1,−5,−10,−0.1-1,-5,-10,-0.1−1,−5,−10,−0.1, and the delay is finite. Hence

y′(∞)=lim⁡s→010e−5s(10s+1)(s+1)(s+5)(s+10)=0.200.y'(\infty)=\lim_{s\to0}\frac{10e^{-5s}}{(10s+1)(s+1)(s+5)(s+10)}=0.200. y′(∞)=s→0lim​(10s+1)(s+1)(s+5)(s+10)10e−5s​=0.200.

For contrast, G(s)=1/(s−1)G(s)=1/(s-1)G(s)=1/(s−1) with a unit step gives y′=et−1y'=e^t-1y′=et−1. The algebraic value G(0)=−1G(0)=-1G(0)=−1 is finite, but the positive pole prevents a final value; using the theorem to claim y′(∞)=−1y'(\infty)=-1y′(∞)=−1 would be invalid.

Link to other topics

Linearisation produces local gains that are derivatives of nonlinear steady relations. Controller decisions require that endpoint information together with transient poles, zeros and delay.

Conclusion

Check settling conditions before evaluating the endpoint. Once they hold, the final-value theorem avoids solving an entire transient just to find its final change.

PDC-20: Local linearisation and reaction-order comparison

Overview

Assumed: Taylor expansion, partial derivatives and reactor balances.

Linearisation replaces a nonlinear model by its tangent dynamics at one operating point. The steady state cancels, while the local slopes become gain and decay coefficients. The approximation is valid for sufficiently small deviations.

Intuition

A curved relationship can look almost straight over a narrow interval. Control near a fixed set point uses that local slope, not a single straight line for every possible operating condition. Moving the operating point can change both sensitivity and response speed.

Derivation

Step 1: define linearity. An operator FFF is linear if F(au+bv)=aF(u)+bF(v)F(au+bv)=aF(u)+bF(v)F(au+bv)=aF(u)+bF(v) for constants a,ba,ba,b. Powers and products of changing variables generally violate this property. A coefficient that depends on time may preserve linearity but loses time invariance.

Step 2: expand a dynamic model. Let output/state yyy obey y˙=f(y,x)\dot y=f(y,x)y˙​=f(y,x) for input xxx. Choose a constant equilibrium (ys,xs)(y_s,x_s)(ys​,xs​) with f(ys,xs)=0f(y_s,x_s)=0f(ys​,xs​)=0; define y′=y−ysy'=y-y_sy′=y−ys​, x′=x−xsx'=x-x_sx′=x−xs​. Taylor expansion gives

y˙′≈f(ys,xs)+fy∣s y′+fx∣s x′=fy∣s y′+fx∣s x′.(61)\dot y'\approx f(y_s,x_s)+f_y|_s\,y'+f_x|_s\,x' =f_y|_s\,y'+f_x|_s\,x'.\tag{61}y˙​′≈f(ys​,xs​)+fy​∣s​y′+fx​∣s​x′=fy​∣s​y′+fx​∣s​x′.(61)

Reason: the constant term vanishes at equilibrium, and terms quadratic or higher in deviations are neglected. Subscripts on fff denote partial derivatives, evaluated at the operating point. With additional disturbance ddd, add fd∣sd′f_d|_s d'fd​∣s​d′; with several states, use the matrix of partial derivatives.

Step 3: expose the local transfer function. Write a=fy∣sa=f_y|_sa=fy​∣s​, b=fx∣sb=f_x|_sb=fx​∣s​. For zero initial deviation,

G(s)=bs−a.If a<0:τ=−1/a,Kp=−b/a.(62)G(s)=\frac{b}{s-a}. \quad\text{If }a<0:\quad \tau=-1/a,\quad K_p=-b/a.\tag{62}G(s)=s−ab​.If a<0:τ=−1/a,Kp​=−b/a.(62)

Reason: transform y˙′=ay′+bx′\dot y'=ay'+bx'y˙​′=ay′+bx′ and isolate the output. The local restoring slope aaa determines the pole. If a=0a=0a=0, the first-order model is an integrator and higher-order terms may be decisive for nonlinear stability.

Step 4: compare reaction orders. For fixed q,V,Tq,V,Tq,V,T and τ=V/q\tau=V/qτ=V/q, first-order consumption gives τc˙A+(1+k1τ)cA=cA0\tau\dot c_A+(1+k_1\tau)c_A=c_{A0}τc˙A​+(1+k1​τ)cA​=cA0​, exactly linear in these concentration variables.

Second-order consumption gives τc˙A+cA+k2τcA2=cA0\tau\dot c_A+c_A+k_2\tau c_A^2=c_{A0}τc˙A​+cA​+k2​τcA2​=cA0​. At its equilibrium, cA0s=cAs+k2τcAs2c_{A0s}=c_{As}+k_2\tau c_{As}^2cA0s​=cAs​+k2​τcAs2​. Substitute cA=cAs+cA′c_A=c_{As}+c_A'cA​=cAs​+cA′​:

τc˙A′+(1+2k2τcAs)cA′+k2τ(cA′)2=cA0′.\tau\dot c_A'+(1+2k_2\tau c_{As})c_A'+k_2\tau(c_A')^2=c_{A0}'. τc˙A′​+(1+2k2​τcAs​)cA′​+k2​τ(cA′​)2=cA0′​.

Reason: expand the square and cancel the steady balance. Neglect the final quadratic term to obtain

G(s)≈1τs+1+2k2τcAs,τlin=τ1+2k2τcAs,Kp=11+2k2τcAs.(63)G(s)\approx\frac1{\tau s+1+2k_2\tau c_{As}},\quad \tau_{lin}=\frac{\tau}{1+2k_2\tau c_{As}},\quad K_p=\frac1{1+2k_2\tau c_{As}}.\tag{63}G(s)≈τs+1+2k2​τcAs​1​,τlin​=1+2k2​τcAs​τ​,Kp​=1+2k2​τcAs​1​.(63)

Reason: the derivative of the reaction sink is 2k2cAs2k_2c_{As}2k2​cAs​, not k2cAsk_2c_{As}k2​cAs​.

To see what the tangent approximation removes, expand (cAs+cA′)2=cAs2+2cAscA′+(cA′)2(c_{As}+c_A')^2=c_{As}^2+2c_{As}c_A'+(c_A')^2(cAs​+cA′​)2=cAs2​+2cAs​cA′​+(cA′​)2. The first term belongs to the equilibrium and cancels; the second changes the local removal slope; the third is the curvature being neglected. A higher positive operating concentration therefore gives a stronger local reaction sink, a shorter time constant and a smaller feed-to-concentration gain. This has the same storage-versus-removal interpretation as the first-order reacting tank, but its coefficients now depend on the operating point.

For a general product of two changing variables, (qs+q′)(cs+c′)=qscs+qsc′+csq′+q′c′(q_s+q')(c_s+c')=q_sc_s+q_sc'+c_sq'+q'c'(qs​+q′)(cs​+c′)=qs​cs​+qs​c′+cs​q′+q′c′. Keep both terms linear in deviations and drop only the final product. Calling the perturbations small is meaningful because their product is smaller in order than either individual deviation; it does not justify discarding one of the linear contributions.

Motivation and explanation

The approximation discards the curvature, not the physical meaning of the original balance. Second-order k2k_2k2​ has units concentration−1^{-1}−1 time−1^{-1}−1; k1k_1k1​ has inverse-time units. Constant-temperature first-order reaction is linear, but a temperature-dependent Arrhenius rate introduces nonlinear coupling if temperature is a changing state.

The neglected quadratic reaction term is small relative to its first-order reaction perturbation when ∣cA′∣≪2cAs|c_A'|\ll2c_{As}∣cA′​∣≪2cAs​. Near cAs=0c_{As}=0cAs​=0, that particular comparison fails and one must inspect the full balance instead. A Taylor model says little about distant equilibria or large excursions.

Worked example

Let τ=100\tau=100τ=100 s, k2=0.0100k_2=0.0100k2​=0.0100 m3^33 mol−1^{-1}−1 s−1^{-1}−1 and cAs=1.00c_{As}=1.00cAs​=1.00 mol m−3^{-3}−3. The corresponding feed equilibrium is cA0s=2.00c_{A0s}=2.00cA0s​=2.00 mol m−3^{-3}−3. Linearisation gives τlin=33.3333\tau_{lin}=33.3333τlin​=33.3333 s and Kp=0.333333K_p=0.333333Kp​=0.333333.

At unchanged operating conditions, a sufficiently small feed-composition increase has one-third of that increase in its final reactor concentration. Linearising about a different cAsc_{As}cAs​ gives different coefficients; this is a local model rather than a globally linear reaction.

The local gain is also the slope of the steady relation. Differentiating cA0s=cAs+k2τcAs2c_{A0s}=c_{As}+k_2\tau c_{As}^2cA0s​=cAs​+k2​τcAs2​ gives dcAs/dcA0s=1/(1+2k2τcAs)dc_{As}/dc_{A0s}=1/(1+2k_2\tau c_{As})dcAs​/dcA0s​=1/(1+2k2​τcAs​). Thus the dynamic linearisation and the tangent to the equilibrium curve predict the same small final change. A finite change follows the curved relation, so this slope need not give its exact endpoint.

Link to other topics

The same Taylor procedure converts a gravity-outflow tank into a lag. Products of valve flow and concentration require it in the three-tank mixing process.

Conclusion

Linearise only after finding a consistent equilibrium. The local derivatives identify the restoring mode and steady sensitivity of small disturbances.

PDC-21: Gravity-draining tank: linear model and exact response

Overview

Assumed: a volume balance and square-root outflow from Bernoulli's law.

Unlike a tank with prescribed pumped withdrawal, a gravity-draining tank has a restoring outflow. Linearisation makes it a local first-order lag; solving the nonlinear step reveals the approximation's limits.

Intuition

A higher level increases the driving head and therefore increases outflow. That feedback in the physics opposes accumulation without a controller. Because outflow increases as a square root, its slope weakens at larger levels; a single tangent model cannot predict every new equilibrium exactly.

Derivation

Step 1: write and linearise the balance. Let area be AAA, level h>0h>0h>0, inlet flow q0q_0q0​, and outlet q=khq=k\sqrt hq=kh​ with fixed valve/outlet coefficient k>0k>0k>0. Assume constant density and area, quasi-steady outflow, no overflow, and no other inflows. Then

Ah˙=q0−kh,q0s=khs.(64)A\dot h=q_0-k\sqrt h,\qquad q_{0s}=k\sqrt{h_s}.\tag{64}Ah˙=q0​−kh​,q0s​=khs​​.(64)

Reason: increasing level stores volume and increases the gravity-driven loss. Define deviations and expand hs+h′≈hs+h′/(2hs)\sqrt{h_s+h'}\approx\sqrt{h_s}+h'/(2\sqrt{h_s})hs​+h′​≈hs​​+h′/(2hs​​). Cancel the steady terms:

Ah˙′=q0′−k2hsh′,τh˙′+h′=Kpq0′,τ=2Ahsk,Kp=2hsk.(65)A\dot h'=q_0'-\frac{k}{2\sqrt{h_s}}h',\qquad \tau\dot h'+h'=K_pq_0', \quad\tau=\frac{2A\sqrt{h_s}}k,\quad K_p=\frac{2\sqrt{h_s}}k.\tag{65}Ah˙′=q0′​−2hs​​k​h′,τh˙′+h′=Kp​q0′​,τ=k2Ahs​​​,Kp​=k2hs​​​.(65)

Reason: the outflow slope supplies a restoring term. The transfer function is G=Kp/(τs+1)G=K_p/(\tau s+1)G=Kp​/(τs+1), with pole −k/(2Ahs)-k/(2A\sqrt{h_s})−k/(2Ahs​​). Gain has units s m−2^{-2}−2, equivalent to level per volumetric-flow change.

Step 2: compare new equilibria. After a step Δq0\Delta q_0Δq0​, the local model gives

hlin′=KpΔq0(1−e−t/τ),hexact,∞′=KpΔq0+(Δq0/k)2.(66)h'_{lin}=K_p\Delta q_0(1-e^{-t/\tau}),\qquad h'_{exact,\infty}=K_p\Delta q_0+(\Delta q_0/k)^2.\tag{66}hlin′​=Kp​Δq0​(1−e−t/τ),hexact,∞′​=Kp​Δq0​+(Δq0​/k)2.(66)

Reason: the exact equilibrium is h∞=[(q0s+Δq0)/k]2h_\infty=[(q_{0s}+\Delta q_0)/k]^2h∞​=[(q0s​+Δq0​)/k]2; subtract hs=(q0s/k)2h_s=(q_{0s}/k)^2hs​=(q0s​/k)2 and expand the square. The missing quadratic term reveals the finite-step error.

2Azz˙=k(zf−z),dt=2Akzzf−z dz.2Az\dot z=k(z_f-z),\qquad dt=\frac{2A}{k}\frac{z}{z_f-z}\,dz. 2Azz˙=k(zf​−z),dt=k2A​zf​−zz​dz.

Reason: substituting the square-root state makes the equation separable. Use z/(zf−z)=−1+zf/(zf−z)z/(z_f-z)=-1+z_f/(z_f-z)z/(zf​−z)=−1+zf​/(zf​−z) and integrate from z0z_0z0​:

Reason: the logarithm comes from integrating 1/(zf−z)1/(z_f-z)1/(zf​−z) with its negative derivative. For a positive inlet step, z0<z<zfz_0<z<z_fz0​<z<zf​.

Step 4: linearise in the transformed state too. Write z=z0+z′z=z_0+z'z=z0​+z′ in 2Azz˙=q0−kz2Az\dot z=q_0-kz2Azz˙=q0​−kz. To first order,

2Az0z˙′+kz′=q0′,h′=2z0z′+O((z′)2).2Az_0\dot z'+kz'=q_0',\qquad h'=2z_0z'+O((z')^2). 2Az0​z˙′+kz′=q0′​,h′=2z0​z′+O((z′)2).

Reason: z′z˙′z'\dot z'z′z˙′ is a second-order perturbation, and the output transformation must also be expanded. Together these recover exactly the earlier local h′h'h′ model. Squaring the approximate z(t)z(t)z(t) without dropping (z′)2(z')^2(z′)2 gives a different finite-step approximation, not the first-order linear level model.

The outlet's local slope is dq/dh∣s=k/(2hs)dq/dh|_s=k/(2\sqrt{h_s})dq/dh∣s​=k/(2hs​​). Dividing area by this slope gives the time constant; the reciprocal of the outflow slope gives the steady level gain. More area slows the response without changing the eventual level needed to pass a given flow. At greater operating depth, the outflow slope is smaller, so an extra inlet flow needs a larger level rise and that rise develops more slowly. These trends follow from the square-root law, not from an assumed universal tank time constant.

For either positive or negative physically admissible inlet changes, the exact final level differs from the tangent prediction by the nonnegative squared term in equation (66). This is the curvature of the equilibrium relation. The transient comparison has to use the same initial level, inlet step and absolute/deviation convention in both models; otherwise a baseline mismatch can look like linearisation error.

Motivation and explanation

The tangent approximation needs ∣h′∣/hs|h'|/h_s∣h′∣/hs​ small. It fails near an empty tank, where the square-root derivative is singular. The coefficient kkk has units m5/2^{5/2}5/2 s−1^{-1}−1, so both the original flow law and the derived time constant are dimensionally consistent.

The exact transient approaches equilibrium asymptotically. A numerical solution of the implicit equation or direct integration can quantify deviations from the local lag without inventing a constant time constant for the nonlinear process.

Worked example

Take A=3.00A=3.00A=3.00 m2^22, k=0.0200k=0.0200k=0.0200 m5/2^{5/2}5/2 s−1^{-1}−1, q0s=0.0200q_{0s}=0.0200q0s​=0.0200 m3^33 s−1^{-1}−1 and Δq0=0.0100\Delta q_0=0.0100Δq0​=0.0100 m3^33 s−1^{-1}−1. Then hs=1.00h_s=1.00hs​=1.00 m, τ=300\tau=300τ=300 s and Kp=100K_p=100Kp​=100 s m−2^{-2}−2. The linear final level is 2.002.002.00 m; the exact final level is 2.252.252.25 m.

At 100010001000 s, the linear model gives h=1.96433h=1.96433h=1.96433 m and direct nonlinear integration gives h=2.13198h=2.13198h=2.13198 m. The implicit solution returns the same nonlinear value. The figure is qualitative; these values are computed from the balances, not read from the plotted lines. The large inlet change demonstrates why local linearisation must be checked for the intended excursion.

The graph illustrates two differences: the local model approaches a different endpoint and follows a different trajectory on the way there. Here the exact final rise exceeds the linear final rise because the true outflow increases less rapidly with level than its initial tangent predicts. To balance the larger feed, the exact model must reach a greater depth. A comparison of settling fractions should therefore use each model's own endpoint.

Link to other topics

Gravity outflow turns an otherwise integrating level into a self-regulating lag. Its steady gain is the derivative of the nonlinear equilibrium relation at the chosen point.

Conclusion

Linearisation preserves the local restoring physics. The exact equilibrium and implicit transient quantify what it loses for a large change.

PDC-22: Three-tank mixing: valve linearisation and step response

Overview

Assumed: component balances, deviation variables, series lags and local linearisation.

A three-tank mixer combines variable-flow nonlinearity with a cascade of concentration lags. The valve and disturbance gains must use a consistent steady composition and an explicit percentage convention.

Intuition

Opening the pure-tracer valve adds tracer, but it also increases total flow and changes residence time. The local model captures the first-order composition effect while dropping products of flow and concentration deviations. Downstream tanks smooth that change twice more.

Derivation

Step 1: define the composition convention and equilibrium. Three perfectly mixed tanks have equal fixed volume V=35V=35V=35 m3^33; their outlet flows follow the combined inlet flow, maintaining each volume. Stream A is pure inert tracer; stream B contains tracer concentration xBx_BxB​ expressed as a numerical volume percent, so pure A has xA=100x_A=100xA​=100, not 111. Assume equal constant densities and additive volumes.

Let flows be qA,qBq_A,q_BqA​,qB​ in m3^33 min−1^{-1}−1, tank volume-percent compositions x1,x2,x3x_1,x_2,x_3x1​,x2​,x3​, and valve position vvv as a numerical percent open. A linear valve gives qA=kvvq_A=k_vvqA​=kv​v, kv=0.0028k_v=0.0028kv​=0.0028 m3^33 min−1^{-1}−1 per percentage point. At vs=50v_s=50vs​=50, qAs=0.14q_{As}=0.14qAs​=0.14; take qBs=6.86q_{Bs}=6.86qBs​=6.86 and xBs=2x_{Bs}=2xBs​=2. Then

1s(τs+1)3=1s−ττs+1−τ(τs+1)2−τ(τs+1)3.\frac1{s(\tau s+1)^3}= \frac1s-\frac{\tau}{\tau s+1}-\frac{\tau}{(\tau s+1)^2}-\frac{\tau}{(\tau s+1)^3}. s(τs+1)31​=s1​−τs+1τ​−(τs+1)2τ​−(τs+1)3τ​.

Reason: multiplying by the common denominator telescopes to one. Inverting the repeated-pole terms gives

x3′=KvΔv[1−(1+tτ+t22τ2)e−t/τ].(71)x_3'=K_v\Delta v\left[1-\left(1+\frac t\tau+\frac{t^2}{2\tau^2}\right)e^{-t/\tau}\right].\tag{71}x3′​=Kv​Δv[1−(1+τt​+2τ2t2​)e−t/τ].(71)

Reason: the third pole contributes the quadratic-in-time exponential term. With τ=5\tau=5τ=5 min, its quadratic coefficient is t2/50t^2/50t2/50.

The first-tank valve gain contains 100−xs100-x_s100−xs​ because each extra unit of pure-tracer inflow also drives out an extra unit of the existing mixture. Counting only the incoming tracer would overstate its effect. In a downstream tank, the baseline inlet and outlet compositions are identical, so changing flow alone creates no first-order composition forcing. It multiplies only the developing composition difference, which is why that contribution is a product of deviations.

Each tank adds one stored concentration and one lag factor. After a valve step, tank 1 begins changing first; its emerging change drives tank 2, which then drives tank 3. The polynomial multiplying the exponential in equation (71) enforces the initially gentle downstream response. A repeated pole describes several sequential memories with the same decay rate, not a single lag with its time constant multiplied by three.

Motivation and explanation

A volume-percent change from 222 to 333 is one percentage point; it is not a 1%1\%1% relative increase. Using volume fractions is equally valid, but requires replacing 100100100 by 111 and rescaling concentration gains consistently.

The cascade has no exact dead time, though its initially flat response can resemble a delay. The local model freezes residence time at its baseline value and is accurate only for small flow/composition changes. A real valve may not be linear in stem position at changing pressure drop.

Worked example

A valve move from 505050 to 606060 percent open has Δv=10\Delta v=10Δv=10 percentage points. The local model predicts a final tracer increase of 0.3841600.3841600.384160 percentage points. At 5.005.005.00 min the increase is 0.03084860.03084860.0308486 points; at 15.015.015.0 min it is 0.2215870.2215870.221587 points.

The final linear prediction is 4.34416%4.34416\%4.34416%. Recomputing the exact steady feed mixture at qA=0.168q_A=0.168qA​=0.168 m3^33 min−1^{-1}−1 gives 4.34263%4.34263\%4.34263%. Their small difference is due to the neglected flow–composition product. The distinction between the baseline 3.96%3.96\%3.96% and a rounded 4%4\%4% must not leave an uncancelled constant term in the derivation.

At one individual tank time constant the final outlet has completed only 8.03014%8.03014\%8.03014% of its own final change; at three it has completed 57.6810%57.6810\%57.6810%. The single-lag 63.2%63.2\%63.2% rule therefore cannot be applied to the whole cascade using τ=5\tau=5τ=5 min. The small difference between exact and linear final compositions checks the local endpoint approximation for this valve move; it does not by itself verify the whole transient.

Link to other topics

This example brings physical balances, local linearisation, transfer-function summation and repeated poles together. These plant-response models are the starting point for designing feedback controllers once a controller model is introduced.

Conclusion

A consistent equilibrium and percentage convention produce a clear local model. Its two input gains and three repeated lag factors separate mixture sensitivity from the dynamics of stored liquid.
